items.title: Holding the Bat: The Knocking-Knuckles Grip
items.objective: The player will be able to pick up a bat and hold it with a relaxed knocking-knuckles grip, bottom hand on the knob end, without being reminded.
items.summary: Where the hands go on the bat, how tight to squeeze, and how to check the grip in two seconds. The first skill every hitter learns.

video.note: Close-up of a six-year-old's hands picking up a bat off the grass, then a slow pan showing the knocking knuckles of both hands lined up along the bat, with the parent checking from behind.

explanation: A grip is simply how your hands hold the bat. The bottom hand is the hand nearest the knob, the little flared end of the bat. For a right-handed hitter the bottom hand is the left hand and the top hand is the right hand; for a left-handed hitter it is the other way around. If your child does not know which way to stand yet, let them pick up the bat and swing it a few times and use whichever side looks more comfortable.

Make a fist and look at the row of knuckles you would knock on a door with. Those are the knocking knuckles. When the bat is held correctly, the knocking knuckles of both hands line up roughly along the bat, so the top-hand knuckles sit between the bottom hand's knocking and big knuckles. The hands touch each other with no gap, and the bottom hand sits about one finger-width above the knob so the knob does not dig into the wrist.

The bat rests in the fingers, not deep in the palms. If you lay a bat across the pads where the fingers meet the hand and close the fingers around it, the grip is right. If the bat is jammed back into the fleshy part of the palm, the wrists lock and the bat cannot whip through. A good test is to have the child wiggle the bat head in small circles; a finger grip lets it move freely.

Grip pressure should be soft. On a scale from one to ten, where ten is squeezing a wet towel dry, the hands should be about a three or four until the swing starts. Tell young hitters to hold the bat like a baby bird or a tube of toothpaste with the cap off. The hands tighten on their own at contact, so there is no need to squeeze early.

Children ages four to eight should use a light bat they can hold straight out in front of them with one hand for five seconds without shaking. A bat that is too heavy forces a palm grip and a long, slow swing. If the only bat you have is heavy, slide both hands up the handle two or three inches, which is called choking up, and the bat will feel lighter.
parentInstructions: Stand behind your child and slightly to the side, never in front. From behind you can see both hands and the knuckles without being anywhere near the bat.

Have your child set the bat on the ground, then bend down and pick it up with both hands. Most children naturally pick it up with the knuckles close to lined up. Praise that, then adjust one hand if needed.
Look at three things only: bottom hand near the knob, hands touching, knocking knuckles roughly in a line. Ignore everything else today.
Ask your child to squeeze the bat as hard as they can and then let go to a three out of ten. Doing this three times teaches what relaxed hands feel like.
Keep the whole session to five minutes for a four- to six-year-old. Check the grip, let them take a few slow practice swings in a clear space, and stop while they still want more.
Use one cue at a time. Say 'knuckles in a line' and nothing else until that is automatic, then move on to 'soft hands'.
Count your child's swings. After eight to ten swings, rest for a minute, shake out the hands, and check the grip again before the next set.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Use a broom handle, a short length of PVC pipe, or a rolled-up magazine taped tight. The knuckle line-up and finger grip can be learned on any stick about an inch thick.
steps: Lay the bat on the ground in a clear area at least twelve feet from walls, cars, pets, and other people.
Have your child pick it up with both hands and lift it to shoulder height. Check that the bottom hand is nearest the knob.

Ask your child to make the hands touch, then look down the bat and see if the knocking knuckles of both hands make a rough line. Gently rotate the top hand if the knuckles point in different directions.
Check that the bat sits in the fingers by having your child wiggle the bat head in a small circle without moving the elbows.
Practice the squeeze-and-release three times: squeeze to ten, let go to three.
Have your child set the bat down and pick it up correctly five times in a row. Celebrate each correct grip.
Finish with five slow, easy practice swings while you watch only the hands from behind. Stop if the grip changes and reset it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hands are crossed, with the top hand nearest the knob.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child set the bat down and pick it up again, saying 'knob hand first' as the bottom hand touches the bat. Do not try to fix it mid-swing.

commonMistakes.mistake: There is a gap between the two hands.
commonMistakes.fix: Slide the top hand down until the hands touch. A gap makes the bat wobble and lets the top hand take over the swing.

commonMistakes.mistake: The bat is buried in the palms so the knuckles point in two different directions.
commonMistakes.fix: Open both hands, lay the handle across the base of the fingers, and close the fingers first, then the thumbs.

commonMistakes.mistake: White knuckles from squeezing too hard.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child shake out both hands, then re-grip at a three out of ten. Remind them the hands get tight on their own when the bat meets the ball.

cues: Hold it like a baby bird
safety: Mark a bat zone with cones, chalk, or a hose: a circle at least twelve feet across that only the hitter stands in. Everyone else, including the parent, stays outside and behind the hitter.
Never check a grip from in front of the child. Walk around behind, fix the hands, and step back out of the bat zone before any swing.
Teach children to set the bat down gently after swinging, never to throw or drop it.
Use a lightweight bat approved for your child's division. Check your league's current Little League rulebook for bat standards.

progression.easier: Skip the swings entirely. Practice only picking the bat up and showing the knuckles, then setting it back down, for ten repetitions.
progression.harder: Have the child close their eyes, pick up the bat, and grip it correctly by feel. Then take three slow swings and freeze so you can check the hands still look the same.

items.title: Athletic Stance and Base Width
items.objective: The player will be able to step into the batter's box and set up in a balanced athletic stance with feet a little wider than the shoulders, knees bent, and weight on the balls of the feet.
items.summary: How a hitter stands before the pitch: foot width, knee bend, where the weight sits, and where the bat waits. A good stance makes every other hitting skill easier.

video.note: A seven-year-old jumps straight up, lands softly in an athletic stance beside a home plate, and a graphic overlay shows the feet just outside the shoulders, bent knees, and the bat resting above the back shoulder.

explanation: The stance is how the hitter stands while waiting for the pitch. Think of how a child stands ready to catch a ball or play goalie: feet apart, knees bent, bottom down a little, ready to move in any direction. That same ready position is the batting stance, just turned sideways to the pitcher with a bat in the hands.

Stand sideways in the batter's box so the front shoulder points at the pitcher. The front foot is the one closest to the pitcher. Spread the feet so the insides of the feet are a little wider than the outsides of the shoulders. For most young children that is about one of their own foot-lengths wider on each side than standing normally. Point both toes at home plate, not at the pitcher.

Bend the knees until the kneecaps are roughly over the laces of the shoes, and let the hips sink an inch or two. Weight stays on the balls of the feet, the padded part just behind the toes, so the heels are light but still touching the ground. A hitter who is on the heels will rock back and fall away from the ball; a hitter who is on the toes will tip forward.

Hold the bat with the hands about even with the back shoulder, four to six inches away from the body, and the bat head angled up and back over the shoulder. The elbows hang down in a relaxed position; the back elbow does not need to be lifted high. The head turns so both eyes are looking at the pitcher, with the chin close to the front shoulder.

Where to stand in relation to home plate matters too. Have the child lay the bat down with the bat head on the far edge of the plate and stand where the knob touches the toes; that puts the plate within reach without crowding it. Put the front foot about even with the middle of the plate so the ball can be hit in front of the body.
parentInstructions: Stand behind your child and off to the side the child faces, at least twelve feet back from the bat. Never stand in front where a bat or ball could reach you.
Look at the feet first. Are they wider than the shoulders? Are both toes pointing at the plate? Fix the feet before you look at anything else.
Next look at the knees. If the legs are straight like a soldier, say 'bend' and gently press down on the top of both shoulders until the knees give a little.
Ask your child to jump up and land. Where they land is almost always a perfect stance width. Use this trick any time the feet drift together.
Check that the bat is up and back over the shoulder, not resting on the shoulder like a lumberjack. A bat lying on the shoulder has a long way to travel.
Keep sessions to six or eight minutes for ages four to six. Set up the stance, take three swings, rest, and set up again. Setting up correctly is the skill; the swings are just the reward.
Praise the stance out loud each time it looks right so your child learns what 'good' means before any ball is involved.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Draw a home plate and two footprints with chalk on the driveway or use two pieces of tape on the floor. The child steps onto the footprints and takes the stance with hands clasped together as if holding a bat.
steps: Mark a home plate with chalk, a paper plate, or a real plate, and clear a bat zone at least twelve feet in every direction.
Have your child stand sideways to an imaginary pitcher with the front shoulder pointing where the pitch would come from.
Say 'jump and stick'. The child jumps straight up and lands softly. Check the feet are a little wider than the shoulders and both toes face the plate.
Say 'bend'. The knees bend until the kneecaps are over the shoelaces and the weight moves onto the balls of the feet.
Have the child lift the bat so the hands are near the back shoulder and the bat head points up and back. Check the elbows are relaxed and hanging.
Ask the child to turn the head and look at the imaginary pitcher with both eyes. Hold the stance for a count of three.
Take one easy practice swing, step out, shake it off, and repeat the set-up from the start five more times.
Finish by having the child set up with eyes closed, then open them and check in a mirror or a photo you take from behind.

commonMistakes.mistake: Feet too close together, so the hitter tips over during the swing.
commonMistakes.fix: Use the jump-and-stick landing to find the width, then draw chalk marks or place tape where the feet landed so the child can step to the same spots every time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing straight up with locked knees.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child pretend to sit on a tall stool behind them. The hips sink an inch or two and the knees unlock. Check that the kneecaps are over the laces.

commonMistakes.mistake: Front foot pointing toward the pitcher, which opens the hips early.
commonMistakes.fix: Turn the front toes to face the plate. Put a small cone or a glove just outside the front foot as a wall the toes must stay behind.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bat resting on the shoulder or hands held down by the belt.
commonMistakes.fix: Lift the hands to shoulder height, about a hand-width off the body, with the bat head angled up and back. Say 'hands up, bat up' before each swing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing so far from the plate that the bat cannot reach the far side.
commonMistakes.fix: Lay the bat across the plate with the bat head on the far edge; the toes go where the knob ends up. Re-measure every time until the spot is automatic.

safety: Set a bat zone at least twelve feet across. The only person inside it is the hitter, and the adult coaches from behind and to the side.
Practice stance work on grass, a mat, or dry pavement, never on a wet or icy driveway where bent knees and bat swings can lead to a slip.
Keep siblings and pets well behind the hitter; a practice swing travels in a full circle around the body.

progression.easier: Practice the stance with no bat at all, hands clasped together, so the child can focus only on the feet and knees.
progression.harder: Have the child set up, then hold the stance while you gently push on the front shoulder and then the back shoulder. A balanced stance does not move.

items.title: Balance Point: Staying Centered Through the Swing
items.objective: The player will be able to take a full swing and hold the finish position for three seconds without stepping, stumbling, or falling toward the plate.
items.summary: A hitter who stays balanced hits the ball harder and more often. This lesson teaches where the weight should be before, during, and after the swing, and how to check it with a frozen finish.

video.note: Side-by-side slow motion of two nine-year-olds: one falls toward the plate after swinging, the other finishes with the head still over the belt buckle and holds the pose for three seconds while a line graphic shows the head barely moving.

explanation: Balance means the hitter's head and weight stay over the middle of the body for the whole swing. Picture a line drawn straight down from the nose to the ground. Before the swing that line lands between the feet. After the swing it should land in almost the same spot, with the head having moved only a few inches toward the pitcher. A swing that ends with the hitter stumbling has sent power into the ground instead of into the ball.

Weight starts spread over both feet, a little more on the back foot, around sixty percent back and forty percent front. During the swing the weight moves against a firm front leg and the back heel comes up so the back foot pivots on the toe. The hips turn, but the head stays nearly still. If you watch only the belt buckle, it should turn to face the pitcher while the head stays where it was.

The front leg is the brake. As the swing starts, the front knee straightens and the front foot presses into the ground so the body cannot keep sliding forward. The back knee drives toward the front knee. Finishing with the back toe touching the ground, the front leg firm, and the chest facing the pitcher is the balanced finish we are after.

The best check is the freeze. After every swing the hitter holds the finish for a slow count of three. If the hitter can hold it, the swing was balanced. If the hitter needs an extra step, wobbles, or tips toward the plate, something pulled the body off center, usually the head flying out or a swing that was too hard for the body to control.

Balance is also about swinging at a speed the body can handle. Most young hitters swing at one hundred percent effort and lose their footing. Ask for a swing at seventy percent, the speed where the freeze is easy, and build up from there. Hard contact comes from a balanced swing far more than from a maximum-effort one.
parentInstructions: Stand behind your child and to the open side, twelve to fifteen feet away. You want to see the head and the feet, so kneel or crouch to get your eyes closer to your child's height.
Watch the head. Pick a spot on a fence or wall directly behind your child's head before the swing and notice how far the head moves from that spot. A few inches is fine; a foot is too far.
Watch the feet at the finish. The back heel should be up with the toe down and the front foot flat and quiet. A front foot that spins open or a back foot that drags forward means balance was lost.
Call out 'freeze' as the bat finishes and count out loud to three. Make a game of it. The child earns a point each time the freeze holds without a wobble.
Keep swings to sets of five with a thirty-second rest between sets so tired legs do not hide the real problem. Ten to fifteen total swings is plenty.
If the freeze keeps failing, ask for a slower swing rather than more effort. Say 'show me a seventy percent swing' and reward the balanced one, not the loud one.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Do the whole lesson as shadow swings with no bat, hands clasped, or with a short stick. The freeze test works exactly the same without equipment.
steps: Clear a bat zone at least twelve feet in every direction and set up a home plate marker.
Have the child take the stance with sixty percent of the weight on the back foot. Ask them to lift the front heel slightly to feel the weight behind them, then set it down.
Take a slow-motion swing with no ball, finishing with the back heel up, back toe down, chest toward the pitcher, and head over the middle. Hold for three seconds.
Repeat the slow-motion swing five times. Only the speed changes; the finish position stays the same.
Take five swings at about seventy percent effort, freezing after each one. Count out loud.
Have the child hold the frozen finish while you gently tap their front shoulder. A balanced hitter does not move.
If a soft ball and tee are available, hit five balls off the tee with the same freeze after each swing, with everyone behind the hitter.
Finish with three swings where the child says 'freeze' themselves before you can.

commonMistakes.mistake: Falling toward the plate after the swing.
commonMistakes.fix: The head is going out ahead of the swing. Have the child finish with the chin close to the back shoulder and the eyes still on the spot where the ball was. Slow the swing until the freeze holds.

commonMistakes.mistake: Spinning on the back foot so the whole body turns and the front foot comes off the ground.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a glove or soft cone just in front of the front foot as a wall it cannot pass. Ask for a firm front leg that pushes back against the swing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Weight stuck on the back foot with the back heel still down at the finish.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child squash an imaginary bug under the ball of the back foot so the heel lifts and the belt buckle turns to the pitcher.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging as hard as possible every time and wobbling.
commonMistakes.fix: Count the balanced swings, not the hard ones, for a week. Build effort back up only when ten freezes in a row hold.

safety: Only the hitter stands inside the bat zone. The parent stays behind and to the side, outside a twelve-foot circle.
Practice on grass or a flat, dry surface so the frozen finish does not become a slip. Wet decks and slick garage floors are not good spots for full swings.
If a tee and ball are added, the child wears a batting helmet and everyone else stands behind the tee, never beside or in front of it.

progression.easier: Practice only the finish. The child steps into the finish position without swinging, holds it for three seconds, and resets. Ten repetitions.
progression.harder: Take swings off a tee and hold the freeze while you roll a ball to the front foot; the hitter should be stable enough to let it bounce off the shoe without moving.

items.title: The Small Load: Getting Ready to Swing
items.objective: The player will be able to make a small, quiet load, shifting weight into the back hip and moving the hands back two to four inches, before every swing without wrapping the bat or lifting the front foot too early.
items.summary: The load is the little backward move a hitter makes right before swinging forward. This lesson teaches a short, repeatable load that stores power without throwing off timing or balance.

video.note: An eleven-year-old shown from the open side in slow motion as the pitcher's arm goes back: the hands drift back about three inches, the front knee turns slightly inward, and the back hip loads, with freeze-frames marking each checkpoint.

explanation: Every athletic move starts with a small move in the opposite direction. A jumper dips before leaving the ground, and a thrower reaches back before coming forward. In hitting that backward move is called the load. It is how the hitter gathers weight and tension so the swing has something to push off from.

A good load is small. From the stance, the hands move back toward the catcher about two to four inches, roughly the width of the hitter's own fist, and stay at the height of the back shoulder. At the same time the weight settles into the inside of the back thigh and the back hip, so the back knee stays bent and points slightly toward the plate rather than bowing out. The front shoulder turns in just a touch, maybe two inches, so the chin brushes the front shoulder.

The front knee gives a clear checkpoint. During the load it turns gently inward toward the back knee, like the hitter is softly pinching a ball between the knees. The front heel can lift, but the front foot does not pick up and leave the ground. That inward knee turn is what coaches mean by coiling, and it keeps the hitter from drifting forward too soon.

The bat barely changes angle. If the bat head wraps around behind the head so the barrel points at the pitcher, the load has gone too far and the swing will be long. The barrel should stay pointed up and slightly back, somewhere between straight up and forty-five degrees. A mirror or a phone video from behind will show this instantly.

Timing the load matters as much as its size. In a game the load begins as the pitcher's arm starts up and finishes as the pitcher's arm reaches its highest point, so the hitter is loaded and still when the ball leaves the hand. For now, practice the load as a slow, deliberate move with a pause at the end so the body learns the position before adding speed.
parentInstructions: Stand behind your child and off to the open side, at least twelve feet from the bat. If you have a phone, film from directly behind the back foot at hip height; that angle shows the hands and the knee at once.
Call 'load' and watch two things: did the hands move back a fist-width and stop, and did the front knee turn in a little? If both happened, say so.
Watch the front foot. It is allowed to lift at the heel but should not step. If the whole foot comes up during the load, the child is striding too early and will lose power.
Check the bat angle by looking at the barrel from behind. If you can see the barrel pointing at the pitcher, the hands have wrapped. Ask for 'barrel up'.
Do loads in sets of six with a pause at the end of each. After the set, let your child shake out the arms and legs for twenty seconds. Fifteen to twenty total loads and ten swings is a full session.
If swings are added, insist on the same small load first. A hitter who loads perfectly in slow motion and then rushes it during a real swing needs more slow repetitions, not more swings.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Hold a rolled-up towel or a short stick in the batting grip. The load is a body movement, so no bat or ball is needed to learn it.
steps: Set up in the athletic stance in a clear bat zone with a plate marker and an imaginary pitcher about forty feet away.
On the word 'load', move the hands back toward the catcher the width of a fist and settle the weight into the back hip. Hold for two seconds.
Check the front knee: it should be turned slightly inward and the front heel light, but the foot still on the ground.
Relax back to the stance. Repeat the load six times, pausing at the top each time, with the parent checking hands, knee, and barrel angle.
Have the child load and then take a slow, half-speed swing, feeling the weight push off the back hip. Repeat five times.
Add a rhythm: the parent slowly raises an arm like a pitcher. The child starts the load as the arm lifts and finishes loaded when the arm is at the top.
Finish with five full-speed shadow swings, each starting from a loaded, paused position, freezing the finish for three seconds.

commonMistakes.mistake: The hands wrap behind the head and the barrel points at the pitcher.
commonMistakes.fix: Load against a wall. Have the child stand with the back about a foot from a wall and load; if the bat taps the wall the load is too long. Keep the barrel between straight up and forty-five degrees.

commonMistakes.mistake: Weight falls to the outside of the back foot and the back knee bows out.
commonMistakes.fix: Place a glove on the ground just outside the back foot. The child loads into the inside of the back thigh so the knee stays over the foot and never leans out toward the glove.

commonMistakes.mistake: The front foot picks up and steps during the load, so the hitter drifts forward too early.
commonMistakes.fix: Practice loads with the front foot flat and only the heel allowed to lift. Add the stride back in only after ten quiet loads in a row.

commonMistakes.mistake: The head moves back with the hands so the eyes bounce.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child fix the eyes on a spot where the pitcher's hand would be. The hands and hips move back, the head stays nearly still.

commonMistakes.mistake: Loading too big and too late, so the body is still moving back when the ball arrives.
commonMistakes.fix: Shrink the hand move to one fist and start it earlier, as the pitcher's arm begins to rise. Small and early beats big and late.

safety: A load leads into a full swing, so keep the twelve-foot bat zone clear and have the parent behind and to the side at all times.
Do slow loads first and build to full speed; a tired hitter rushing full-speed swings is the most likely to lose the bat.
Check the ground around the back foot for loose gravel or wet grass, since the load puts extra weight on that foot.

progression.easier: Remove the bat and do the load with hands clasped, focusing only on the back hip and front knee for ten repetitions.
progression.harder: Have a partner call 'load' at random moments while the hitter watches an imaginary pitcher, then immediately swing off a tee into a net, keeping the load the same size every time.

items.title: Stride and Separation
items.objective: The player will be able to take a short, soft stride of two to six inches straight toward the pitcher while the hands stay back, landing on the inside of the front foot with the front shoulder still closed.
items.summary: The stride is the small step toward the pitcher, and separation is keeping the hands back while that step happens. Together they create the stretch that makes a swing quick and strong.

video.note: Overhead and side views of a ten-year-old striding onto a chalk line while a rolled towel held between the hands stays back near the shoulder, with an overlay showing the growing distance between the front foot and the hands.

explanation: The stride is a short step with the front foot toward the pitcher. It is not a lunge and it is not a kick. For most Little League hitters it is somewhere between two and six inches, which is less than the length of the hitter's own shoe. The foot lands softly on the inside edge, the big-toe side, with the toes still pointing at the plate or only slightly open toward the pitcher. Landing with the toes turned toward the pitcher opens the hips too soon.

Separation is the stretch between the lower body and the hands. As the front foot moves forward, the hands stay back near the back shoulder or even drift back another inch. That means the front foot is going one way and the hands are staying put, so the distance between them grows. A hitter can feel this as a stretch across the front of the chest and the inside of the front thigh.

A simple picture helps: a rubber band. The stride stretches the band, and the swing is the band snapping. If the hands come forward with the stride, the band never stretches and the swing is all arms. If the hands stay back as the foot lands, the hips can fire first and pull the hands through, which is where bat speed comes from.

The stride should land before the swing starts. Picture the sequence as three separate beats: load, stride and land, then swing. When the front foot lands, the weight is still mostly back, about sixty percent on the back leg, the head is centered, and the front shoulder still points at the pitcher. Only after the foot is down does the back hip fire and the swing begin.

Direction is the last checkpoint. The stride goes straight at the pitcher, not toward the plate and not away from it. Stepping away from the plate, which coaches call stepping in the bucket, pulls the front shoulder open and makes outside pitches impossible to reach. A chalk line or a flat strip of tape on the ground from the front toe toward the pitcher gives the hitter a target to land on every time.
parentInstructions: Stand behind your child and off to the open side, twelve to fifteen feet away, so you can see the front foot and the hands at the same moment.
Draw a chalk line or lay a strip of tape from your child's front toe straight toward the imaginary pitcher. Every stride should land on or beside that line, never off to the side away from the plate.
Watch the hands while the foot moves. If the hands drift forward with the step, say 'hands stay home'. The hands should not move toward the pitcher until the foot is flat on the ground.
Check the landing foot. The heel comes down softly and the toes still face the plate. If the toe points at the pitcher on landing, ask the child to land on the big-toe side of the foot.
Run sets of six strides with no swing, then six strides with a slow swing. Rest a minute between sets and stop after three or four sets.
Avoid coaching the whole move at once. Pick one checkpoint per set, such as the line, the hands, or the landing foot, and say nothing about the others.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Use a rolled bath towel held in the batting grip. The towel shows whether the hands stay back during the stride and can be swung safely indoors.
steps: Mark home plate and draw a straight line from the front toe toward the pitcher. Clear a bat zone twelve feet around the hitter.
From the stance, load as taught in the small load lesson, with hands back a fist-width and weight in the back hip.
Lift the front foot an inch and stride forward two to six inches along the line, landing softly on the inside of the foot. The hands stay back. Freeze there for two seconds.
Check the frozen position: weight mostly back, front shoulder closed, hands near the back shoulder, toes facing the plate. Reset and repeat six times.
Now add a slow swing after the freeze. Land, pause, then swing at half speed and hold the finish. Repeat six times.
Shorten the pause so the sequence becomes load, land, swing with no stop, but still at an easy speed. Repeat six times.
If a tee, net, and soft balls are available, hit six balls with the same three-beat rhythm, with everyone behind the hitter.
Finish by having the child stride with eyes closed three times and open them to see whether the foot landed on the line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stepping in the bucket, away from the plate.
commonMistakes.fix: Place a glove or soft cone where the foot keeps landing so the child must step along the chalk line instead. Have the child look at an outside pitch location while striding to remind them where the ball will be.

commonMistakes.mistake: A long stride of a foot or more that drops the head and pulls the weight forward.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a strip of tape six inches in front of the toe as the farthest the foot may go. Count 'one' for the stride and 'two' for the swing to separate them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hands come forward with the stride, so there is no stretch.
commonMistakes.fix: Hold a towel between the hands and stride while you lightly hold the far end of the towel behind the hitter; the child should feel a gentle tug as the foot lands.

commonMistakes.mistake: Landing on the heel with the toe open toward the pitcher.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask the child to land on the big-toe side of the shoe with the heel floating for a split second, then settle. Practice ten soft landings without a swing.

safety: Striding with a bat is a full-swing drill. Keep the parent behind and to the side and the twelve-foot bat zone clear of siblings and pets.
Use chalk or flat tape for the line, never a rope, cord, or stick the hitter could trip over.
A batting helmet goes on as soon as a ball is added, even off a tee at a team station where several hitters are swinging.

progression.easier: Remove the stride entirely and practice a no-stride load with the front heel lifting and setting back down in the same spot while the hands stay back.
progression.harder: Have a partner toss a soft ball underhand from the side into a net. The hitter must land the stride before the toss arrives and still keep the hands back until the foot is down.

items.title: Swing Path: Short to the Ball
items.objective: The player will be able to swing the knob of the bat toward the ball first so the barrel takes a short, direct path to contact instead of a long loop.
items.summary: The swing path is the road the bat travels to the ball. A short, direct path gets the barrel there on time and hits more line drives than a big loop.

video.note: A nine-year-old swings in slow motion from the catcher's view with the bat path traced as a glowing line, comparing a long loop that drops the barrel below the ball with a short, direct path where the knob leads and the barrel arrives level through the hitting zone.

explanation: The swing path is the route the bat travels from the shoulder to the ball. There are two common paths. The long path drops the barrel down behind the back shoulder and swoops it around and up, like a big hook. The short path leads with the knob, the end of the handle, straight toward the ball while the barrel stays above the hands until the last moment, then whips through. The short path takes less time, which gives the hitter more time to see the pitch.

A useful way to feel the short path is to think about where the knob points. From the loaded position, the knob points down toward the ground behind the hitter. The first move of the swing drives the knob toward the pitcher's side of the plate, toward where the ball will be, while the hands stay close to the body. For a right-handed hitter, that means the hands pass about a fist-width from the ribs as they come forward.

The back elbow is the key joint. As the swing starts, the back elbow drops down and slides in toward the back hip, which pulls the knob forward. The hands follow the elbow. If the back elbow stays high and the hands reach out toward the pitcher early, the barrel flings away from the body and the path gets long.

The barrel should arrive at the ball on a slight upward path that matches the slight downward angle of the pitch, which means close to level through the hitting zone. Imagine a table at the height of the pitch; the bat slides along that table for the last foot before contact and the first foot after. A bat that chops down through the table or swoops up from under it has only an instant of contact time and will produce weak ground balls or pop-ups.

Young hitters do not need to think about all of this at once. The two cues that fix most swings are 'knob to the ball' and 'back elbow to the hip'. If the knob goes to the ball and the hands stay tight, the barrel path takes care of itself.
parentInstructions: Stand directly behind your child, twelve to fifteen feet back, as if you were the catcher far behind the plate. From behind you can see whether the barrel drops below the hands or stays above them.
Watch the first six inches of the swing only. The knob should move toward the pitcher and the hands should stay close to the body, like the child is pulling a lawnmower cord toward their belly.
Look at the back elbow. It should tuck down toward the back hip as the swing starts, not fly up and away.
Ask for half-speed swings first. The path is impossible to see at full speed. Ten slow swings teach more than fifty fast ones.
Use the clasped-hands drill with no bat at the start of each session so your child can feel the path without the weight of the bat pulling the hands into a loop.
Give one cue at a time, either 'knob to the ball' or 'elbow to the hip', and praise every swing where the barrel stays above the hands early.
Rest after every eight swings. A tired hitter drops the barrel, and that is not a path problem to fix, it is a sign to stop for the day.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Clasp both hands together like one fist and swing them along the path, leading with the pinky side of the bottom hand toward the ball. This is a real drill that coaches use and needs no equipment at all.
steps: Clear a twelve-foot bat zone. Begin with no bat: clasp the hands, take the stance, and load.
Swing the clasped hands slowly to an imaginary ball out in front of the front hip, feeling the back elbow slide to the back hip first. Repeat eight times.
Pick up the bat and hold the loaded position. Have the parent point to where the ball would be, about even with the front foot at belt height.

Move the knob toward that spot at half speed, stopping when the hands reach the front hip and the barrel is still behind the hands. Check the position, then finish the swing slowly. Repeat eight times.
Take eight half-speed swings without stopping, freezing only at the finish. The parent watches the first six inches.
If a tee, net, and soft balls are available, set the tee at belt height even with the front foot and hit eight balls with the same short path, everyone behind the hitter.
Finish with three full-speed shadow swings and a frozen finish on each.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping the barrel below the hands right away and swinging up at the ball, producing pop-ups.
commonMistakes.fix: Place a second, empty tee or a tall cone a foot behind the ball tee and two inches higher. A barrel that drops early clips the cone. Hit slowly until the cone is untouched for five swings.

commonMistakes.mistake: Casting, where the hands fly out away from the body and the swing becomes a wide arc.
commonMistakes.fix: Stand the child a bat-length plus a fist from a soft net and take half swings. Hands that cast will touch the net. Keep the hands inside so the bat clears the net.

commonMistakes.mistake: Chopping straight down at the ball like an axe, producing weak ground balls.
commonMistakes.fix: Raise the tee to chest height for ten swings so the child feels a level path through the ball, then return to belt height.

commonMistakes.mistake: Back elbow stays high and the hands push forward instead of the knob leading.
commonMistakes.fix: Hold the child's back elbow lightly from behind and guide it to the back hip in slow motion three times, then let them repeat it alone.

safety: The parent coaches from behind, never from in front or beside the hitter, since a short path drill involves full swings.
When using a net and tee, check that the net is at least fifteen feet from the hitter and that the barrel cannot reach walls, cars, or windows on the follow-through.
Use only soft or safety balls off the tee in driveways and garages, and wear a batting helmet whenever a ball is in play.

progression.easier: Do only the clasped-hands swing with no bat for the whole session. Add the bat another day.
progression.harder: Hit off the tee set at three heights, knee, belt, and chest, keeping the barrel above the hands early on all three. Add the empty-tee obstacle behind the ball.

items.title: Hip Rotation: Using the Lower Half
items.objective: The player will be able to start the swing by turning the hips and pivoting the back foot so the belt buckle faces the pitcher at contact while the hands follow the hips instead of leading them.
items.summary: Power does not come from the arms. This lesson teaches a hitter to turn the hips first, pivot the back foot, and let the hands come along for the ride.

video.note: A twelve-year-old holding a bat across the lower back in the crooks of both elbows turns the hips to face the pitcher while the back heel lifts, then the same hitter swings off a tee with a slow-motion overlay showing the belt buckle turning before the hands move.

explanation: The lower half means everything from the belt down: hips, legs, and feet. The biggest, strongest muscles in a young body are there, so a swing that uses them will always be stronger than a swing that uses only the shoulders and arms. Hip rotation is the act of turning the hips toward the pitcher to start the swing.

Start from the landed stride position, with the front foot down and the hands still back. The first thing that moves is the back hip, which drives forward and around toward the pitcher. To let that happen, the back foot pivots on the ball of the foot so the heel lifts and turns out, the way you would squash a bug under your toe. The back knee turns in and points toward the front knee.

The front side is the post. The front leg firms up and the front hip stops turning, so the back hip has something to rotate against. By contact the belt buckle should face the pitcher squarely. If a parent stands far behind the pitcher's spot, they should be able to read the whole belt buckle at the moment the bat meets the ball.

The hands come last. Because the hands are connected to the shoulders, and the shoulders sit on top of the hips, turning the hips pulls the hands into the swing without the hitter having to throw them. Hitters who swing with their arms first leave the hips facing the plate and lose most of their power. A good checkpoint is that the hips start to open while the hands are still back near the shoulder.

Keep the head still through all of it. The hips turn underneath the head like a lazy Susan spinning under a bowl. If the head turns with the hips, the eyes leave the ball. A hitter who can rotate fully while the head stays over the middle of the body has learned to use the lower half.
parentInstructions: Stand well behind your child and to the open side, twelve to fifteen feet back. For the belt-buckle check, you can also stand far out where the pitcher would be, at least forty feet away, only when the child is doing shadow swings with no ball.
During the bat-behind-the-back drill, watch the back heel. It should lift and turn out as the hips rotate. A heel stuck flat on the ground means the hips are not turning.
Watch the order of movement during slow swings. Hips first, then shoulders, then hands. If the hands move before the hips, say 'hips start it'.
Look at the belt buckle at the finish. It should face the pitcher. If it still faces the plate, the swing was all arms.
Do eight hip turns with the bat behind the back, then eight slow swings, then rest for a minute. Three rounds is plenty.
Say 'squish the bug' for the back foot and 'belt buckle to the pitcher' for the hips. Choose one for the session and stick with it.
Keep the head still as a separate check for another day. Trying to fix the hips and the head in the same session is too much.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Hold a broom handle, a towel, or just clasp the hands behind the lower back and practice the hip turn with the back foot pivot. The feeling is identical without a bat.
steps: Clear a bat zone twelve feet around and set a plate marker. Begin with the bat held horizontally across the lower back, hooked in the crooks of both elbows.

Take the stance and stride. On 'turn', rotate the hips toward the pitcher, lifting the back heel and pivoting on the ball of the back foot until the bat across the back points at the pitcher. Hold for two seconds.
Repeat the hip turn eight times, checking the belt buckle faces the pitcher and the head stays centered.
Take the bat out and hold it normally. Do eight slow swings where the parent counts 'hips' on the first beat and 'hands' on the second.
Do eight half-speed swings with no counting, freezing at the finish with the back heel up and the belt buckle to the pitcher.
If a tee, net, and soft balls are available, hit eight balls focusing only on the hips starting the swing, everyone behind the hitter.
Finish with three full-speed shadow swings. Freeze and check the back foot and belt buckle each time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging with the arms while the hips stay facing the plate.
commonMistakes.fix: Go back to the bat-behind-the-back turn for ten repetitions, then take swings at half speed where the hitter says 'hips' out loud as the swing starts.

commonMistakes.mistake: Back foot stays flat and the heel never lifts.
commonMistakes.fix: Place a soft ball or a crumpled paper cup under the back heel in the stance so the hitter is already on the ball of the foot and can pivot freely.

commonMistakes.mistake: Spinning so hard the front foot opens and the whole body turns past the pitcher.
commonMistakes.fix: Firm up the front leg and put a glove just outside the front foot as a wall. The front hip stops, the back hip turns to meet it.

commonMistakes.mistake: The head turns with the hips so the eyes leave the contact point.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child stare at a ball on a tee through the whole shadow swing, finishing with the eyes still on the ball and the chin near the back shoulder.

safety: The bat-behind-the-back drill swings the bat ends around the body, so hitters at a team station need at least eight feet between them.
Full swings follow this drill, so the parent stays behind and to the side and the twelve-foot bat zone stays clear.
Do the pivot on a surface with grip, such as grass or dry pavement; a back-foot pivot on wet or sandy ground can slip.

progression.easier: Do the hip turn with no bat and the hands on the hips so the child can feel the hips move with their own hands.
progression.harder: Hit off a tee with the back foot starting on its toe, heel already lifted, which forces the hips to carry the swing. Then try a slow side soft toss into the net with the same hips-first feel.

items.title: Hands Inside the Ball
items.objective: The player will be able to keep the hands between the body and the ball through the swing, so an inside pitch can be hit hard to the pull side without the barrel swinging out and around.
items.summary: Keeping the hands inside the ball means the hands travel a tight path close to the body while the barrel stays behind them. It is how good hitters handle inside pitches and stay on outside ones.

video.note: A fourteen-year-old takes swings a bat-length from a hanging net, first casting the hands so the bat brushes the net, then keeping the hands inside so the bat clears it, followed by inside-tee swings with the hands traced as a tight line close to the body.

explanation: Picture a straight line from the pitcher to the catcher running through the middle of home plate. A pitch travels along a line like that. Hands inside the ball means that as the swing comes forward, the hands stay on the body side of the ball's path, between the hitter and the ball, while the barrel trails behind the hands. The barrel only passes the hands at the moment of contact.

The opposite is casting, where the hands move out away from the body at the start of the swing and the barrel swings around in a wide arc. A cast swing is slow because the barrel has farther to go, and it gets jammed on inside pitches because the barrel reaches the hitting zone too early and too far out. A hands-inside swing can let the ball travel deeper and still hit it on the barrel.

The move that keeps the hands inside is the same back elbow drop from the short swing path, but held longer. As the hips start the swing, the back elbow drops into the slot next to the back hip and the hands slide forward along the body, about a fist-width from the ribs. The knob leads toward the inside half of the ball. At contact on an inside pitch, the hands are well out in front of the body and the barrel is just getting to the ball, which is why the inside pitch gets pulled.

A hitter with the hands inside can hit every pitch location with the same hand path. On an inside pitch the barrel gets out front and pulls the ball. On an outside pitch the hands stay inside longer and the barrel meets the ball deeper, sending it the other way. The hands do the same thing both times; only the timing of when the barrel releases changes.

The net drill is the clearest test. Stand with the plate a bat-length plus a fist from a soft net or hanging blanket, so the net is where the pitcher's side of the plate would be. Swing. A cast swing hits the net on the way to the ball; a hands-inside swing clears it. This is a feel drill, not a power drill, so swings are at seventy percent until the net stays untouched.
parentInstructions: Stand behind your child, twelve to fifteen feet back, where you can see the hands and the net at the same time. Never stand beside the net or in the gap between the hitter and the net.
In the net drill, listen as much as you watch. The sound of the bat brushing the net tells you the hands cast, even if you could not see it.
Watch the hands pass the ribs. They should travel about a fist-width from the body as the swing starts. Hands that drift out to a foot away are casting.

On inside-tee swings, look at where the ball goes. A hands-inside swing pulls the ball hard to the side the hitter faces away from; a cast swing produces weak hits toward the opposite side or off the handle.
Keep swings in sets of six with a minute of rest. The feel fades when the hitter tires, so twenty-four total swings is a good session.
If the bat touches the net three times in a row, drop to half speed and have the child do the clasped-hands version until the feel comes back.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Hang a blanket or a bedsheet from a clothesline or a fence and use it as the net. If there is no bat, clasp the hands and do the drill with the pinky side of the bottom hand leading past the blanket.
steps: Set a home plate marker so its pitcher-side edge is one bat length plus a fist from a soft net or hanging blanket. Check that there is fifteen feet of clearance in every other direction.
Take the stance and load with no ball. Swing slowly at half speed, leading with the knob and keeping the hands a fist-width from the body. Notice whether the bat touches the net.
Repeat eight half-speed swings until the bat clears the net five times in a row.
Move to seventy percent speed for eight swings. Freeze each finish and check the net is still.
Set a tee so the ball is on the inside third of the plate, even with the front foot, belt high. Put the net fifteen feet in front as the hitting target.
Hit eight soft balls off the inside tee with the hands inside, aiming to pull the ball hard into the net. Everyone else stands behind the hitter.
Move the tee to the outside third, deeper in the zone near the middle of the plate, and hit eight balls the other way with the same hand path.
Finish with four swings back at the net-distance spot to confirm the feel held.

commonMistakes.mistake: Casting the hands away from the body so the bat brushes the net.
commonMistakes.fix: Hold a batting glove or a folded towel under the back armpit during slow swings. If it falls before contact, the back elbow and hands flew out.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rolling the top hand over before contact so the barrel swings around the ball.
commonMistakes.fix: Hit the inside tee with the palm of the top hand facing up at contact, like serving a tray. Hold the finish for two seconds to check the top palm.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling the front shoulder out early to make room for the inside pitch.
commonMistakes.fix: Keep the front shoulder closed and let the back elbow drop into the slot instead. The room for the inside pitch comes from the elbow, not the shoulder.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the inside pitch travel too deep and getting jammed on the handle.
commonMistakes.fix: Move the inside tee two inches farther in front of the front foot so the hitter learns that inside contact happens out front.

cues: Knob to the inside of the ball
safety: Use a soft net, blanket, or sheet for the net drill, never a chain-link fence, a wall, or a wooden fence that could send the bat bouncing back.
The parent stands behind the hitter, never between the hitter and the net or beside the net where a misjudged swing could reach.
A batting helmet is worn for all tee swings, and the fifteen-foot bat zone in front of the hitter stays empty.
Hands-inside swings put the bat close to the body, so make sure the hitter's elbows and wrists are warmed up with ten easy shadow swings first.

progression.easier: Do the net drill with clasped hands and no bat, then with a short training bat or a bat choked up to the middle of the handle.
progression.harder: Alternate inside and outside tee balls without telling the hitter which is next until they step in. The hands must take the same path either way.

items.title: Finishing the Swing: Extension and Follow-Through
items.objective: The player will be able to extend both arms through the ball after contact and finish with the bat wrapped high around the back while staying balanced over the front leg.
items.summary: What happens after the bat hits the ball still matters. A full extension and a high, relaxed finish mean the bat was accelerating through the ball instead of slowing down to meet it.

video.note: A ten-year-old hits off a tee into a net in slow motion, with freeze frames at contact, at full arm extension with the bat pointing at the pitcher, and at the high finish with the bat over the front shoulder and the back toe down.

explanation: Extension is what the arms do right after the bat meets the ball. Both arms straighten out toward the pitcher so the bat head keeps moving through the spot where the ball was, as if the hitter is trying to hit three balls in a row lined up toward the pitcher's mound. A hitter who stops the bat at contact has been slowing down before the ball arrived. A hitter who extends has been speeding up.

The checkpoint for extension is a position coaches call the power V. A moment after contact, both arms are nearly straight and form a V shape with the bat pointing out toward the pitcher or slightly to the pull side. The top hand palm faces the sky and the bottom hand palm faces the ground. From behind, a parent should see the bat head out beyond the front foot before it starts to come around.

The follow-through is where the bat ends up. After full extension the arms bend again and the bat wraps around the body, finishing high over the front shoulder or behind the neck. Some hitters let go with the top hand after the power V and finish with one hand; others keep both hands on the bat. Either is fine for a Little League hitter as long as the release happens after extension, not before.

Balance holds through the whole finish. The weight has moved onto a firm front leg, the back foot is up on its toe, the belt buckle faces the pitcher, and the head is still over the middle of the body looking at the contact point. The finish should be relaxed; a hitter who finishes with tight, jerky arms was muscling the bat instead of letting it swing.

A good follow-through cannot rescue a bad swing, but a bad follow-through almost always reveals one. Chopping down and stopping, pulling the bat across the body low, or finishing with the weight on the back foot are all signs that the earlier parts of the swing need work. That is why we check the finish on every swing in every drill.
parentInstructions: Stand behind your child and to the open side, at least twelve feet back from the bat. Crouch so your eyes are at your child's shoulder height and watch the bat head after contact.

Look for the power V a split second after contact: both arms nearly straight, bat pointing toward the pitcher. If the elbows are still bent and the bat is already wrapping around the body, the swing stopped short.
Check the finish height. The bat should end up above the front shoulder or behind the neck, not down by the hip.
Ask your child to hold the finish for a count of three. Use that frozen moment to check the front leg is firm, the back heel is up, and the head has stayed over the middle.
Tee work for this lesson runs in sets of six swings with a minute of rest, three or four sets total. Pick up the balls yourself between sets so your child stays behind the tee.
Say 'hit three balls in a row' or 'throw the barrel at the pitcher'. Pick one cue and keep it for the whole session.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Take shadow swings and freeze at the power V, then at the high finish. A rolled towel swung into an imaginary ball also shows extension because the towel snaps out straight when the arms extend.
steps: Set the tee at belt height with the ball even with the front foot, fifteen feet from a net, in a bat zone cleared twelve feet around. The hitter wears a batting helmet and all other people wait behind the tee.
Take five shadow swings, stopping each one at the power V: arms extended, bat pointing at the pitcher, top palm up. Have the parent check each one.
Take five more shadow swings all the way to a high finish, holding for three seconds.
Hit six balls off the tee, trying to hit through three imaginary balls in a line toward the net. Freeze the finish after each.
Rest for a minute while the parent collects the balls. Talk about which swings felt like the bat was still speeding up at contact.
Hit six more balls, this time with the parent calling 'reach' right at contact to encourage extension.
Hit a final six with no cues at all. The child checks their own finish and says 'good' or 'short' after each swing.
Finish with three one-handed shadow swings with the bottom hand only, letting the arm extend fully to feel the reach.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping the bat at the ball so the finish is low and short.
commonMistakes.fix: Place a second ball on the ground six inches in front of the tee toward the pitcher. The hitter tries to swing far enough to have hit that second ball too.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting go with the top hand before extension, so the bat flips around early.
commonMistakes.fix: Keep both hands on the bat for the whole follow-through for a week of tee work. Release can come back later once extension is automatic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Finishing with the weight on the back foot and the chest leaning back.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child finish with the chest over a firm front leg and the back toe barely touching. Freeze and check that the back heel is high.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arms extend but the head pulls up and out to watch the ball fly.
commonMistakes.fix: Finish every swing with the eyes still on the tee for a full second before looking up. Count 'one' before the eyes move.

cues: Hit three balls in a row
safety: Everyone other than the hitter stands behind the tee and outside the twelve-foot bat zone. The high finish swings the bat all the way around the body.
Hit only into a net or open space with nobody within sixty feet in the direction of the net. Check that the net is anchored and will not tip back toward the hitter.
Use soft or safety balls in driveways and garages, and a batting helmet for every tee swing.

progression.easier: Hit off the tee at half speed with the only goal of holding a three-second finish, ignoring where the ball goes.
progression.harder: Move to side soft toss into the net with the same power V checkpoint, or raise the tee to chest height so the extension must happen on a higher plane.

items.title: Eyes on Contact: Tracking the Ball
items.objective: The player will be able to keep both eyes on the ball from the tee or the tosser's hand all the way to the bat, and keep the head down at the contact spot after the swing.
items.summary: Young hitters miss the ball because their eyes leave it. This lesson uses games with colored and numbered balls to teach children to watch the ball the whole way and keep the head still.

video.note: A five-year-old watches a soft ball with a colored dot roll off a parent's hand, shouts the color, and catches it, then hits a ball off a tee while the camera stays on the child's face to show the eyes staying down on the tee after contact.

explanation: Hitting starts with the eyes. If the eyes see the ball all the way to the bat, the hands have a good chance of getting the bat there. If the eyes jump away to look where the ball might go, the head moves, the shoulders follow, and the bat misses. The most common reason a young child swings and misses is that they looked up before the bat got to the ball.

Tracking means following the ball with both eyes, not just turning the head toward it. In the stance the head turns so both eyes face the pitcher or the tee. Most children naturally tuck one eye behind the nose; ask them to turn the chin a little more so both eyes can see. A quick test is to have the child cover one eye and then the other while looking at the ball; if either eye cannot see it, the head needs to turn more.

On a tee the ball is not moving, so the job is simpler: stare at a spot on the ball before the swing, keep staring at that spot through contact, and keep the eyes on the tee for a count of one after the ball is gone. We say 'see the ball hit the bat' even though it happens too fast to really see, because trying to see it keeps the head down and still.

When a ball is tossed or rolled, the eyes have to pick it up early, right out of the tosser's hand, and ride along with it. Games help. Balls with colored dots or big numbers written on them let the child prove they were watching by calling out what they saw. A child who calls the right color as the ball arrives was tracking; a child who guesses was not.

Four- to eight-year-olds learn this best in short, playful bursts. Five minutes of color-call games, a few tee swings with the head staying down, and lots of praise beat twenty minutes of corrections. One cue, 'eyes on the ball', is enough for the whole lesson.
parentInstructions: For tee work stand behind your child and off to the side, about twelve feet away. Watch the face, not the ball. If the chin lifts before the bat reaches the ball, say 'eyes on the tee'.
For the color-call game, there is no bat involved, so you can kneel ten feet in front of your child and roll or toss a soft ball underhand. Use balls with colored dots or numbers written in marker.
Ask your child to shout the color or number the moment they see it. Praise a correct call even if the catch is dropped; the eyes are the skill today.
Check both eyes can see the ball. Have your child set up, then cover one eye with your hand from behind and ask if the ball is still visible, then switch eyes. Turn the chin until both work.
Keep the tee portion to ten swings total, in two sets of five, with a quick rest to collect balls. Stop while your child is still having fun.
Only one cue today: 'eyes on the ball'. Do not mention the grip, the stance, or the swing even if they look wrong.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Use a rolled-up pair of socks or a tennis ball with numbers drawn on in marker for the color-call game. For the head-still part, the child points at an imaginary ball on a tee and swings with clasped hands, keeping the eyes on the spot.
steps: Write big numbers or draw colored dots on three or four soft balls. Have your child stand ready with no bat.
Kneel ten feet away and roll a ball toward your child's feet. The child calls the number or color as early as possible, then picks up the ball.
Switch to gentle underhand tosses at chest height. The child calls the color, then catches or traps the ball against the chest. Do ten tosses.
Set up the tee at belt height with the ball even with the front foot. Helmet on, everyone else behind the hitter, bat zone cleared twelve feet around.
Have your child pick a dot or a letter on the ball and stare at it for a count of two before swinging.
Swing and keep the eyes on the tee until you say 'look'. Do five swings, collect the balls, and repeat for five more.
Finish with the color-call game again as a reward, this time with the child calling the color before the ball is halfway.

commonMistakes.mistake: Looking up to see where the ball went before the bat arrives.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a small sticker on the tee's rubber top. After each swing the child must tell you what color the sticker is before looking up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only one eye on the ball because the chin is tucked behind the front shoulder.
commonMistakes.fix: Turn the chin until it rests just over the front shoulder with both eyes facing the ball. Use the cover-one-eye test to confirm.

commonMistakes.mistake: Head pulls off toward the pitcher side as the swing starts.
commonMistakes.fix: Have your child swing at half speed and finish with the chin on the back shoulder and the eyes still on the tee for a count of one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Guessing the color instead of watching the ball during the toss game.
commonMistakes.fix: Slow the toss down, shorten the distance to six feet, and hold the ball still for two seconds before tossing so the child can see the color leave your hand.

safety: The color-call game uses soft or safety balls only and no bat, so it is safe indoors and in small yards.
During tee swings the parent and any siblings stand behind the hitter, outside a twelve-foot circle, and the hitter wears a batting helmet.
Hit tee balls into a net or open grass with nobody within sixty feet in front of the hitter.
Never toss a ball toward a child who is holding a bat in this lesson; the tossing games and the tee swings are kept completely separate.

progression.easier: Only roll balls on the ground for the color-call game and skip the tee swings until the child can call five colors in a row.
progression.harder: Move the color-call game to soft tosses from the side into a net with the child holding a bat and calling the color before swinging, as taught in the soft toss lesson.
