items.title: Contact Point: Hitting the Ball Out Front
items.objective: The player will be able to meet the ball at the correct contact point for each pitch location, out in front of the front foot for inside pitches, even with the front foot for middle pitches, and deeper near the middle of the plate for outside pitches.
items.summary: Where the bat meets the ball decides whether the hit is hard and fair. This lesson teaches the three contact points and how to feel them with a tee and a marker on the ground.

video.note: Overhead view of a home plate with three contact points marked by colored discs, and an eleven-year-old hitting a tee ball from each spot in slow motion while the ball flies to the matching part of the field.

explanation: The contact point is the exact spot where the bat meets the ball. Get it right and the barrel is square to the ball with the arms almost extended, which is where a hitter is strongest. Too far back and the hitter is jammed, with bent arms and the ball hitting the handle. Too far out front and the barrel has already passed the best spot, so the ball rolls weakly to the pull side.

The contact point moves depending on where the pitch is. Picture home plate split into three strips running from the pitcher to the catcher: inside, middle, and outside. For an inside pitch the ball must be hit well out in front, about a foot ahead of the front foot, so the barrel has time to get around. For a middle pitch the contact point is about even with the front foot's instep. For an outside pitch the ball is allowed to travel deeper, to a spot somewhere between the front foot and the middle of the plate, and it is hit to the opposite field.

Think of the three points as a diagonal line. Inside is out front and toward the pull side; middle is even with the front foot over the heart of the plate; outside is deeper and over the far edge of the plate. If a parent lays three paper plates or chalk marks on the ground at those spots, the hitter can see the diagonal and move the tee from spot to spot.

At the right contact point the arms are almost but not quite straight, the top hand palm faces up and the bottom hand palm faces down, the hips have turned so the belt buckle faces the pitcher on an inside pitch or faces the shortstop area on an outside pitch, and the head is down looking at the ball. The barrel is slightly above or level with the hands, never dropped far below them.

Contact point is one of the two reasons hitters foul balls off. If the ball keeps going foul to the pull side, the contact was too far out front. If it keeps going foul the other way or hits the handle, contact was too deep. Watching where the fouls go tells the hitter and the parent which way to move the contact point.
parentInstructions: Stand behind your child and off to the open side, twelve to fifteen feet back from the tee. Crouch low; the contact point is easier to see with your eyes at the ball's height.

Before the first swing, mark three spots on the ground with chalk, paper plates, or flat discs: a foot in front of the front foot on the inside edge, even with the front instep over the middle, and halfway back to the middle of the plate on the outside edge.

Move the tee to one of the three spots for each set and tell your child which pitch it represents. Watch where the ball goes. Inside should go to the pull side, middle up the middle, outside to the opposite field.
Look at the arms at contact. Almost straight is right. Arms bent to ninety degrees means the ball was too deep, and fully locked with the barrel already turned means too far out front.
Run three sets of six swings, one set at each spot, with a minute of rest between sets while you collect the balls. Keep your child behind the tee while you do it.

If every ball goes to the same place no matter where the tee is, the contact point is not moving. Slow the swings down and have your child point the bat at the ball on the tee before each swing to notice where it is.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Mark the three contact spots with chalk and take shadow swings, stopping the bat at each marked spot with the arms nearly straight to feel the difference between out front, even, and deep.
steps: Set the plate marker and clear a twelve-foot bat zone with a net fifteen feet toward the pitcher. The hitter puts on a helmet and everyone else lines up behind the plate.
Mark the three contact points on the ground with chalk or discs: inside and out front, middle even with the front instep, outside and deeper.
Put the tee on the middle spot at belt height. Take three shadow swings stopping the bat at the ball with arms nearly straight to feel the spot.
Hit six balls from the middle spot into the center of the net. Freeze each finish and check the belt buckle faces the net.
Move the tee to the inside spot, a foot in front of the front foot. Hit six balls, pulling them to the pull-side part of the net.
Move the tee to the outside spot, deeper and on the far edge of the plate. Hit six balls to the opposite-field side of the net, letting the arms extend toward that side.
Mix the three spots in any order for a final six swings, with the child saying the location out loud before each swing.
Finish by pointing out where any foul-direction misses went and which way the contact point should move next time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hitting every pitch at the same spot, so outside pitches get pulled weakly and inside pitches jam the hitter.
commonMistakes.fix: Say the location out loud before every swing and move the tee a full foot between spots so the difference is obvious. Smaller moves come later.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the outside pitch get too deep and fouling it off the other way or hitting the handle.
commonMistakes.fix: Move the outside tee two inches forward toward the pitcher until the ball flies into the net on the opposite side, then slowly bring it back.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reaching out for the outside pitch with the arms while the hips stay back.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child feel the hips turn toward the opposite field at contact so the body, not the arms alone, takes the barrel to the ball.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hitting the tee stem instead of the ball when the tee is moved out front.
commonMistakes.fix: Raise the tee an inch, slow down, and have the child look at the top half of the ball. A barrel that drops under the ball clips the stem.

safety: Only the hitter stands inside the twelve-foot bat zone. The parent moves the tee between sets while the hitter rests the bat on the ground and stands back.
Hit only into a net or open space with nobody within sixty feet in front of the hitter, and use soft or safety balls near houses and cars.
Wear a batting helmet for every tee swing, including at team stations where several hitters are working side by side.

progression.easier: Work only the middle contact point for the whole session until six balls in a row go straight into the net.
progression.harder: Have a partner toss soft balls underhand from the side to the three locations in random order, and the hitter must adjust the contact point on the fly, as taught in the soft toss lesson.

items.title: Timing Off a Pitcher: Starting on Time
items.objective: The player will be able to start the load as the pitcher's arm starts up, land the stride as the ball leaves the hand, and be on time for a medium-speed pitch without rushing or being late.
items.summary: Good mechanics mean nothing if the swing starts at the wrong moment. This lesson gives hitters a simple rhythm to time their load and stride to the pitcher's motion.

video.note: Split screen of a coach throwing front toss from behind an L-screen and a twelve-year-old hitter, with a rhythm counter showing the hitter's load beginning as the arm goes back and the stride landing exactly as the ball is released.

explanation: Timing means starting the swing at the right moment so the barrel reaches the contact point at the same instant the ball does. A hitter with perfect mechanics who starts late will foul the ball off or miss. A hitter who starts too early will be out in front, off balance, and weak. Timing is a rhythm, and like any rhythm it can be practiced.

The hitter's clock is the pitcher. Every pitcher does the same thing before releasing the ball: the hands separate, the throwing arm swings down and back, then up, and the ball leaves the hand near the top. Hitters use that motion as a countdown. The rule for most Little League pitchers is: begin the load when the pitcher's arm starts to come up, and have the stride foot landing as the ball leaves the hand.

A rhythm of three words helps young hitters feel this. 'Yes' as the arm starts up and the hitter loads. 'Yes' as the ball leaves the hand and the stride foot lands. 'Go' or 'no' as the ball crosses the decision point, roughly halfway to the plate, when the hitter either swings or holds. Every pitch gets a 'yes, yes' no matter what, so the hitter is always ready; only the last word changes.

Being early is better than being late. A hitter who is loaded and landed with the hands back can wait for a slow pitch, because the hands have not moved yet. A hitter who is late has to rush everything, and rushing is where swings fall apart. If a pitcher is slow, the fix is to wait longer with the hands back after landing, not to start the load later.

Pitchers in games will have different speeds and different windups, so hitters should practice the rhythm against a variety of tossers. A parent throwing underhand front toss from behind a screen, a coach throwing overhand batting practice, and a pitching machine all need the same three-beat rhythm, just started at slightly different moments. Watching the pitcher's arm, not the pitcher's face or feet, keeps the clock accurate.
parentInstructions: If you are the tosser, you must be protected. Throw underhand front toss from fifteen to twenty feet from behind an L-screen, a protective net with a cut-out that you throw through, or use very soft sponge balls if no screen is available. Never throw to a hitter from the open with real baseballs.

Make your toss motion big and repeatable: hold the ball up where the hitter can see it, swing your arm down and back, then release on the way up. The hitter needs a motion to time, so do not flip the ball quickly from your hip.
Say the rhythm out loud at first: 'yes' as your arm goes back, 'yes' as you release, and let your child say 'go' or 'no'. After a few rounds, stop saying it and see if the rhythm holds.
Watch the stride foot. It should land as the ball leaves your hand. Landing after the ball is halfway means the child is late; landing before your arm starts means too early.
Throw in sets of eight with a minute of rest. Twenty-four to thirty tosses is a full session, and your child should only swing at the good ones.
Mix in a few deliberately slow tosses. Praise your child for staying back and waiting with the hands rather than lunging. That is the whole lesson in one moment.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: The parent stands forty feet away and mimes a pitching motion with no ball while the child shadow swings on the rhythm. A rolled sock ball tossed from behind a couch or a piece of furniture works for very light indoor rhythm practice with a towel instead of a bat.
steps: Set up on a field or a large yard with at least forty feet of open space in front of the hitter and nobody in it. Helmet on the hitter.
The tosser sets the L-screen fifteen to twenty feet from the plate and stands behind it with a bucket of soft balls. Any other players stand behind the hitter or well behind the screen.
Start with no ball. The tosser mimes the toss motion while the hitter loads on the first 'yes', strides on the second 'yes', and shadow swings on 'go'. Do eight.
Toss eight balls at an easy, consistent speed with the rhythm said out loud by the tosser. The hitter swings only at tosses in the strike zone.
Toss eight more with no words. The hitter says 'yes, yes, go' or 'yes, yes, no' silently and swings on the good ones.
Mix in two or three slower tosses without warning. The hitter must land the stride and wait with the hands back.
Finish with eight tosses at the normal speed and have the hitter report after each one whether they felt early, late, or on time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting the load when the ball is already in the air, so everything is rushed.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the hitter say 'yes' out loud the moment the tosser's arm starts back, even before the ball is visible. If the word is late, the load is late.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lunging forward at slow pitches instead of waiting with the hands back.
commonMistakes.fix: Throw three slow tosses in a row and have the hitter land the stride, then count 'one' before swinging. The hands stay back during the count.

commonMistakes.mistake: Watching the ball only after it leaves the hand instead of watching the arm.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the hitter track the tosser's hand from the moment it holds the ball up and call out when the arm starts back. The eyes pick up the ball earlier that way.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging at every toss, including balls out of the zone, because the body is already moving.
commonMistakes.fix: Make 'yes, yes, no' a success. Count held swings on bad tosses as points, so the hitter learns that being loaded and holding is normal.

safety: Anyone throwing to a hitter must be behind an L-screen, or must be using soft sponge or safety balls at a distance of at least fifteen feet. Hard baseballs are never thrown to a hitter from the open at any age.
The hitter wears a batting helmet, and all waiting players stand behind the hitter and outside the bat zone, never beside the plate or near the screen.
Use a field or park with at least forty feet of clear space in front of the hitter and nothing breakable in the flight path.
Tossers throw underhand or easy overhand and stop after thirty tosses to rest their own arm.

progression.easier: Practice the rhythm against a mimed motion with no ball, then against balls rolled or tossed to a spot the hitter does not have to swing at, just land on time.
progression.harder: Have the tosser vary speed on every pitch without a pattern, or move to a pitching machine or live coach pitch where the hitter must find the rhythm of a new arm.

items.title: Tee Work Basics: Setting Up the Tee Correctly
items.objective: The player will be able to help set the tee at belt height, stand the right distance from it with the ball even with the front foot, and hit a soft ball off the tee without hitting the tee itself.
items.summary: A batting tee is the best teacher a young hitter has, but only if it is set up right. This lesson covers tee height, where the hitter stands, and the first hits.

video.note: A parent and a five-year-old set up a tee together on a driveway, adjusting the height to the child's belt, laying the bat across the plate to find the standing spot, and hitting three soft balls into a net while the parent stands behind and to the side.

explanation: A batting tee is a rubber stem on a base that holds the ball still at a height the hitter chooses. It is the safest and most useful hitting tool there is, because the ball does not move, so the child can think about one thing at a time. Tee ball games are played entirely off a tee, and older players keep using tees for their whole careers.

Set the height so the ball sits at the hitter's belt when they are in their bent-knee stance, not when standing straight up. If the child stands tall to be measured and then bends their knees to hit, the ball will suddenly be at chest height and the swing will chop down. Have the child take the stance first, then adjust the tee so the middle of the ball is level with the top of the pants.

Where the tee sits matters as much as how high it is. Put the plate down first, then place the tee so the ball is over the middle of the plate and even with the hitter's front foot. Many tees have a home plate built into the base; the ball should sit toward the front edge of that plate, not in the middle of it, because the plate on the base sits where real home plate would be and contact happens in front of it.

To find the standing spot, have the child lay the bat down with the fat end touching the ball and stand where the knob reaches their toes, then step back about one shoe length. From there the stance is the same as always: feet wider than the shoulders, knees bent, hands up and back. The child should be able to touch the ball with the bat head by extending the arms, and nothing more.

Hitting the tee instead of the ball is the most common frustration. It usually means the barrel dropped under the ball, the tee is too low, or the child is standing too close. Raising the tee half an inch, stepping back a few inches, and telling the child to look at the top half of the ball fixes almost all of it. Young children need to hear that hitting the tee is normal and that nobody is upset about it.
parentInstructions: Set the tee up together. Let your child turn the adjustment and push the ball on. Children who help set up are more patient when they miss.

Once the tee is set, stand behind your child and to the side the child faces, about twelve feet away, and stay there. Never walk in front of the tee to fix the ball while the bat is in your child's hands.
To reset the ball, say 'bat down' first. Your child sets the bat on the ground and takes a step back before you walk to the tee.
Look at only two things: is the ball at the belt, and is the ball even with the front foot? If both are right, let the swings happen without more coaching.
Hit in sets of five. After five balls, say 'bat down', collect the balls together, give a high five, and go again. Three sets, fifteen swings, is a full session for a four- to six-year-old.
Use a soft or safety ball, never a hard baseball, for tee work with young children at home. The ball can come off the bat quickly even from a small hitter.
Celebrate contact of any kind. A ball that dribbles three feet counts as a hit today.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Stack two or three upside-down buckets or a traffic cone to belt height and set a tennis ball or rolled sock ball on top. A plastic bat or a broom handle works for first swings with a sock ball.
steps: Pick a flat spot with at least forty feet of open grass in front and twelve feet clear all around, or set a net fifteen feet in front on a driveway. Put the plate down first.
Have your child take the batting stance next to the plate. Adjust the tee so the middle of the ball is at the top of the pants.
Place the tee so the ball is over the middle of the plate and even with your child's front foot.
Have your child lay the bat down with the barrel touching the ball, stand where the knob meets the toes, and step back one shoe length. Mark the back foot spot with chalk.
Helmet on. Everyone else moves behind the hitter and outside the bat zone.
Hit five soft balls, saying 'bat down' before each reset. Collect the balls together.
Check the tee height again, since tees shift, and hit five more. Finish with a third set of five and a celebration of the best hit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Tee set too high because the child was measured standing straight up.
commonMistakes.fix: Measure only in the bent-knee stance. If the child keeps standing tall, hold a hand at belt height and set the ball level with your hand.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ball placed over the middle of the plate behind the front foot, so the child hits it too deep and hits the tee.
commonMistakes.fix: Slide the whole tee forward until the ball is even with the front foot's instep, then re-mark the back foot spot.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing too close so the bat handle hits the ball.
commonMistakes.fix: Re-measure with the bat laid across the plate and step back one shoe length. Draw the foot spot in chalk so it stays.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hitting the tee stem over and over and getting upset.
commonMistakes.fix: Raise the tee half an inch, have the child look at the top half of the ball, and say that everyone hits the tee sometimes. Take one slow swing that stops at the ball before the next real swing.

cues: Look at the top of the ball
safety: Only the hitter stands inside a twelve-foot bat zone. The parent coaches from behind and to the side and resets the ball only after the bat is on the ground.
Use soft or safety balls, a batting helmet, and a net or open space with nobody within sixty feet in front of the hitter.
Keep siblings, pets, and bystanders behind the hitter, and never let anyone fetch a ball in front while another child is holding a bat.
Check the tee base is flat and stable; a wobbly tee tips into the hitter's feet.

progression.easier: Use a bigger, lighter ball such as a soft playground ball or a foam ball on the tee so contact is almost guaranteed, and let the child hit without a helmet rule only if no other children are nearby and the ball is foam.
progression.harder: Move the tee to knee height and then chest height for a few swings each so the child learns to adjust, as taught in the next tee lesson.

items.title: Tee Work: Inside, Middle, and Outside Pitch Locations
items.objective: The player will be able to hit tee balls set on the inside, middle, and outside thirds of the plate to the matching part of the field, adjusting contact point and barrel direction without changing the swing.
items.summary: Moving the tee around the plate turns one drill into a full hitting lesson. Hitters learn to pull the inside pitch, drive the middle pitch, and take the outside pitch the other way.

video.note: A ten-year-old hits three tee balls in a row from inside, middle, and outside locations into a wide net marked with left, center, and right zones, shown from behind the hitter so the viewer sees the ball fly to the matching zone each time.

explanation: Once a hitter can set up a tee and hit the ball off it, the tee becomes a tool for practicing every pitch a real pitcher will throw. Pitches come inside, down the middle, and outside, and each location has its own best place to hit the ball. The tee lets the hitter practice each one hundreds of times without needing a pitcher.

Divide the plate into three strips. The inside strip is the third closest to the hitter. For an inside pitch the tee moves toward the hitter and forward, so the ball sits about a foot in front of the front foot. The hitter pulls this pitch, meaning a right-handed hitter hits it toward left field and a left-handed hitter toward right field. The barrel has to get out in front to do that, so the hips turn fully and the belt buckle faces the pitcher.

For a pitch down the middle the tee sits over the middle of the plate with the ball even with the front foot's instep. The hitter drives this pitch back up the middle toward where the pitcher would be. For an outside pitch the tee moves to the far edge of the plate and back toward the catcher, so the ball sits between the front foot and the middle of the plate. The hitter lets this pitch travel and hits it to the opposite field, with the hips turning only part way and the barrel reaching out and across.

The swing itself does not change. The hands take the same path, the hips start the swing, and the head stays still. What changes is when the barrel is released and where contact happens. Hitters who try to make a different swing for each location get tangled up; hitters who keep one swing and move the contact point get hits everywhere.

A wide net or an open field lets the hitter see the results. If the inside tee ball flies to the opposite field, the barrel was late and the contact point was too deep. If the outside tee ball gets pulled, the hitter got out front too early. The ball's direction is the report card, and the fix is always to move the contact point, never to swing harder.
parentInstructions: Stand behind your child and to the open side, twelve to fifteen feet back from the tee, where you can see both the tee location and where the ball goes.
Mark the three tee locations on the ground with chalk before starting so you can move the tee quickly between sets. Inside is toward your child and forward; outside is away and back.
Call out where the ball went after each swing: 'pull side', 'middle', or 'other way'. Your child learns to connect the location to the result without you explaining mechanics.
Watch the hips on the outside tee. They should turn only part way, toward the opposite field, not all the way to the pitcher. On the inside tee they should turn all the way.

Run three sets of six, one per location, then a fourth set of six where you move the tee to a random spot after each swing. Rest a minute between sets while you collect balls with the bat on the ground.
If more than two balls in a set go the wrong direction, move the tee an inch or two in the direction that helps and say nothing about the swing.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Chalk the three locations and take shadow swings to each, stopping the bat at the ball spot to feel the barrel pointing toward the pull side, up the middle, or to the opposite field.
steps: Set the plate, clear a twelve-foot bat zone, and place a wide net fifteen feet in front or use an open field. Helmet on the hitter; the rest of the group waits behind the plate marker.
Chalk three tee spots: inside and a foot in front of the front foot, middle even with the front instep, outside on the far edge and back toward the middle of the plate.
Set the tee on the middle spot at belt height. Hit six balls up the middle into the center of the net. Freeze and check the finish each time.
Move the tee to the inside spot. Hit six balls to the pull side of the net with the hips turning all the way to the pitcher.
Move the tee to the outside spot. Hit six balls to the opposite-field side of the net, letting the ball travel and the barrel reach across.
For the final set, move the tee to a random spot after each swing. The hitter says the location out loud before swinging and the parent calls where the ball went.
Finish with a quick count of how many balls went to the matching side of the net out of the last six.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling the outside tee ball because the hitter gets out front too early.
commonMistakes.fix: Move the outside tee two inches farther back toward the catcher and say 'let it travel'. Have the hitter aim at the opposite-field corner of the net.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hitting the inside tee ball weakly to the opposite field because the barrel is late.
commonMistakes.fix: Move the inside tee two inches farther forward and cue the hips to turn all the way so the belt buckle faces the pitcher at contact.

commonMistakes.mistake: Changing the whole swing for each location, with a chopping swing inside and a reaching swing outside.
commonMistakes.fix: Go back to the middle tee for six swings to reset the one swing, then move to the other spots with the same rhythm and finish.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning the upper body toward the outside tee instead of turning the hips toward the opposite field.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child keep the head over the middle and feel the back hip push toward the far corner of the net. Place a glove outside the front foot to stop any drift.

commonMistakes.mistake: Clipping the tee stem on the inside location.
commonMistakes.fix: Raise the inside tee half an inch, since contact out front is naturally a little higher, and have the child look at the inside top of the ball.

safety: The parent moves the tee between sets only after the hitter has set the bat on the ground and stepped back out of the twelve-foot bat zone.
Use a wide, anchored net or an open field with nobody within sixty feet in any direction the ball could fly, since outside tee balls go to the opposite field.
A batting helmet is worn for all tee swings, and at team stations tees are spaced at least fifteen feet apart with all hitters facing the same direction.

progression.easier: Use only the middle and outside spots for a week before adding the inside spot, which needs the most hip turn.
progression.harder: Add the two-tee obstacle on the inside spot by placing an empty tee a foot behind the ball tee, or move to side soft toss to the three locations as the tosser calls them.

items.title: Soft Toss and Front Toss Progression
items.objective: The player will be able to hit soft tosses from the side into a net with a full, balanced swing, then progress to underhand front toss from behind a screen while keeping the same swing.
items.summary: Soft toss adds a gently moving ball to the swing the hitter built on the tee. This lesson shows the safe tosser positions, the toss itself, and the steps from side toss to front toss.

video.note: A parent kneels on the open side of a nine-year-old and diagonally ahead of the plate, tossing soft balls underhand into a net while the child hits, then the camera shows the move to underhand front toss from behind an L-screen fifteen feet away.

explanation: Soft toss is when a tosser kneels off to the side of the hitter and flips a ball underhand into the hitting zone, and the hitter drives it into a net. The ball is moving slowly and arrives at a known spot, which makes it the perfect step between the tee and a real pitch. Front toss comes next: the tosser kneels directly in front of the hitter, protected by a screen, and tosses underhand from fifteen to twenty feet so the hitter sees the ball coming from the pitcher's direction.

The tosser's position for side toss is the key safety and quality point. The tosser kneels on the open side, the side the hitter's chest faces, about ten to twelve feet away and a step or two ahead of the plate toward the pitcher. From there the toss travels across the hitter's body into the contact zone in front of the front foot, and the ball is hit straight ahead into the net, away from the tosser. The tosser is never straight in front of the hitter and never behind the plate.

The toss itself is a soft underhand flip with a small arc, released from about knee height so the ball peaks around the hitter's chest and drops into the zone at belt height even with the front foot. A good toss is slow enough that the hitter can load, stride, and swing with rhythm. A rushed, flat toss turns the drill into a reaction test and ruins the swing. Tossers should show the ball, drop the hand, and flip in a steady count so the hitter can time it.

The hitter's job is the same swing as the tee: load as the tosser's hand drops, stride as the ball leaves the hand, and swing through the ball with a frozen finish. Because the ball now moves, the eyes have to pick it up out of the tosser's hand and follow it in, so the tracking lesson matters here. Hitters who look at the net or the tosser's face instead of the ball will swing under it.

Front toss changes only the direction the ball comes from. The tosser kneels behind an L-screen, a tall net with a cut-out on one side, fifteen to twenty feet in front of the plate and tosses underhand through the cut-out. Now the hitter sees the ball coming the way a pitch does and the contact points from the tee lessons apply directly. Hitters should master side toss, with eight out of ten hard hits into the net, before moving to front toss.
parentInstructions: Set the net first, fifteen feet in front of the plate, and make sure it is anchored. Then kneel on the side your child's chest faces, ten to twelve feet away, a step or two ahead of the plate. You should be looking at your child's front shoulder, not their back.
Toss underhand with a small arc so the ball drops to belt height even with the front foot. Count 'one, two' in your head as you show the ball and flip it so your rhythm never changes.
Watch two things: did the eyes follow the ball into the bat, and did your child hold a balanced finish? Everything else can wait.
Toss in sets of eight with a minute of rest while you collect balls together. Twenty-four tosses is a full home session.

Move to front toss only when you have an L-screen or are using very soft sponge balls. From behind the screen, kneel so your head and body are fully behind the netting and toss underhand through the cut-out.
If swings get wild, go back to the tee for five balls, then return to soft toss. Jumping between the two keeps the swing honest.
Never let siblings or teammates stand near you as the tosser or in front of the hitter. Everyone waiting stands behind the hitter.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Hang a blanket or bedsheet on a clothesline as the net and toss rolled sock balls or crumpled paper balls from the side. The hitter can use a plastic bat or a broom handle; the rhythm and tracking are identical.
steps: Set an anchored net fifteen feet in front of the plate with twenty feet of clear space around the hitter. Batting helmet on; waiting players line up behind the hitter, never near the tosser.
The tosser kneels on the open side, ten to twelve feet away and a step ahead of the plate, with a bucket of soft balls.
Toss three balls with no swing. The hitter tracks each one into the zone and lets it drop, saying 'yes' when it reaches the contact point.
Toss eight balls at a steady rhythm. The hitter loads as the hand drops, strides as the ball leaves, and drives it into the net with a frozen finish.
Rest, collect balls together, and toss a second set of eight, calling out where each ball hit the net.
If eight of ten in the last set were hit hard, set up the L-screen fifteen feet in front and toss four balls underhand through the cut-out for the hitter to track without swinging.
Toss eight front tosses for the hitter to drive back up the middle. Freeze the finish on each.
Finish with three tee balls to end on a still ball and a good swing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging under the ball and popping it up because the eyes are on the net instead of the ball.
commonMistakes.fix: Toss three balls with no swing and have the child watch each one into the zone and call 'yes'. Then toss for real and have them say the color of the ball at contact.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the swing because the toss is too fast or flat.
commonMistakes.fix: The tosser slows down, adds a little arc, and counts 'one, two' out loud so the hitter has a rhythm to follow.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reaching across the body toward the tosser instead of waiting for the ball to arrive out front.
commonMistakes.fix: Move the tosser a step farther ahead of the plate so the toss arrives in front of the front foot, and remind the hitter to let the ball come to the zone.

commonMistakes.mistake: Losing the tee swing and swinging with all arms once the ball moves.
commonMistakes.fix: Alternate three tee balls and three tosses for a full set so the body carries the hips-first swing from one to the other.

cues: Watch it out of the hand
safety: The side tosser kneels on the open side, ten to twelve feet away and ahead of the plate, never directly in front of the hitter and never behind the plate. The hit ball goes straight ahead into the net, away from the tosser.
Front toss is done only from behind an L-screen, or with very soft sponge balls at fifteen feet or more if no screen is available. Hard baseballs are never front tossed without a screen.
The hitter wears a batting helmet, uses soft or safety balls near houses and driveways, and everyone waiting stands behind the hitter outside the twenty-foot zone.
Soft toss and front toss belong in yards, parks, and fields, not garages, because the tosser shares the space with a swinging bat and flying balls.

progression.easier: Toss larger, slower balls such as a soft playground ball or a foam ball from six feet, and let the child hit into open grass with nobody in front.
progression.harder: The tosser calls 'inside', 'middle', or 'outside' and tosses to that location so the hitter adjusts the contact point, or moves to overhand coach pitch as taught in the moving-ball lesson.

items.title: Bat Control: Top-Hand and Bottom-Hand Drills
items.objective: The player will be able to hit tee balls with each hand alone on a choked-up bat, keeping the barrel on a short path, so that both hands do their separate jobs in the full swing.
items.summary: Each hand has its own job in the swing. One-hand drills teach the bottom hand to pull the knob and the top hand to deliver the barrel, and they fix swings that are all top hand or all bottom hand.

video.note: An eleven-year-old choked halfway up the bat hits tee balls into a net with the bottom hand only, then the top hand only, with slow-motion overlays showing the knob leading on bottom-hand swings and the palm-up barrel delivery on top-hand swings.

explanation: Bat control is the ability to put the barrel exactly where the hitter wants it. The two hands have different jobs in doing that. The bottom hand, the one nearest the knob, pulls the knob toward the ball and steers the direction of the swing. The top hand delivers the barrel to the ball and keeps it from dropping or rolling over too early. When one hand takes over, the swing suffers in a predictable way.

A swing that is all top hand rolls over early. The top hand gets strong and turns the barrel so the wrists roll before contact, producing ground balls to the pull side and a barrel that sweeps around the ball. A swing that is all bottom hand pulls off and gets long. The barrel drags behind, the hitter is late, and the ball goes weakly the other way or is fouled off. One-hand drills isolate each job so the hitter can feel it.

Bottom-hand swings use a bat choked up to the middle of the handle or a lighter training bat. The hitter sets up normally, takes the top hand off and tucks it behind the back or on the chest, and swings with the bottom hand only from a tee set at belt height. The knob leads, the arm stays slightly bent until contact, and the barrel comes through on a short path with the elbow finishing near the belly. The swing is at about half speed; this is a feel drill.

Top-hand swings use the same choked-up bat with only the top hand on it. The hitter sets up with the bat at the back shoulder, the top-hand elbow down near the ribs, and swings by driving the elbow to the hip and then the palm toward the ball, palm facing up at contact. The barrel stays above the hand until the last moment. It is harder than it looks, so the tee may need to be raised an inch and the swing slowed down.

After each round of one-hand swings, the hitter puts both hands back on and takes normal swings, trying to feel both jobs happening at once: the bottom hand pulling the knob and the top hand delivering the barrel palm-up. Most hitters feel an immediate difference in how connected the swing is. Done once or twice a week, these drills keep the hands balanced for the whole season.
parentInstructions: Stand behind your child and to the open side, twelve to fifteen feet from the tee. One-hand swings are slower and shorter, but the bat zone rule does not change.
Have your child choke up so the top of the grip is at least halfway up the handle. A full-length grip with one hand is too heavy and will teach a long, slow swing.
On bottom-hand swings, watch the knob. It should move toward the ball first, and the elbow should finish bent near the belly rather than flung out straight.
On top-hand swings, watch the palm at contact. It should face the sky. If it is already turned over toward the ground, the wrist rolled early.
Run sets of five with each hand, then five with both hands, and rest a minute. Three rounds is plenty; forearm fatigue sets in quickly on one-hand swings and the drill stops helping.
Tell your child in advance that one-hand swings feel weak and awkward at first. The ball only needs to travel ten feet into the net for the drill to work.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Do one-hand shadow swings with a short stick or a rolled towel, stopping at the contact spot to check the knob lead on bottom-hand swings and the palm-up position on top-hand swings.
steps: Set the tee at belt height even with the front foot, fifteen feet from a net, with a cleared twelve-foot bat zone. Helmet on, others behind.
Choke up to the middle of the handle. Take five bottom-hand-only shadow swings at half speed, knob leading, elbow finishing near the belly.
Hit five tee balls with the bottom hand only, aiming for a short path and a line drive into the net. The free hand rests on the chest.
Take five top-hand-only shadow swings, driving the elbow to the hip and the palm to the ball, palm up at contact.
Hit five tee balls with the top hand only. Raise the tee an inch if the barrel keeps dropping under the ball.
Put both hands on, still choked up, and hit five tee balls feeling both jobs at once. Freeze each finish.
Rest, collect balls together, and repeat the whole sequence twice more. Finish with five full-grip swings off the tee.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a full-length grip with one hand so the barrel drags and the swing gets long.
commonMistakes.fix: Choke up to the middle of the handle or switch to a shorter, lighter bat. The barrel should feel light enough to stop at the ball.

commonMistakes.mistake: Top hand rolls over before contact, sending ground balls to the pull side.
commonMistakes.fix: Hit top-hand tee balls while holding the finish with the palm facing up for two seconds, then carry that feel into two-hand swings.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bottom-hand swing becomes a long sweep with the arm locked straight.
commonMistakes.fix: Keep the bottom elbow bent until contact and finish with the elbow near the belly. Slow to half speed until the path shortens.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging too hard with one hand and losing the bat.
commonMistakes.fix: Cut the effort in half; the ball only has to reach the net. Rest the forearm between sets and stop at fifteen one-hand swings per hand.

safety: One-hand swings are easier to lose, so the bat zone stays cleared twelve feet around and the parent stays behind and to the side.
Stop one-hand work at fifteen swings per hand per session to protect young wrists and forearms, and skip the drill if the hitter reports soreness.
Wear a batting helmet, use soft or safety balls, and hit only into an anchored net or open space with nobody in front.

progression.easier: Do only shadow swings with each hand and no ball, then hit a bigger foam ball off the tee with each hand.
progression.harder: Have a partner side-toss soft balls into the net for one-hand swings, or alternate one bottom-hand, one top-hand, and one two-hand swing off tees set at three locations.

items.title: Bunting Fundamentals
items.objective: The player will be able to square around on time, hold the bat level at the top of the strike zone with the top hand pinching behind the barrel, and deaden a tossed ball down either baseline.
items.summary: A bunt is a soft tap that rolls the ball a few feet into fair territory. This lesson covers the pivot, the bat position, the hand placement that keeps fingers safe, and where to aim.

video.note: A ten-year-old pivots into bunting position as a coach tosses from behind an L-screen, with a close-up of the top hand pinching the bat behind the barrel and the ball dying ten feet up the third-base line.

explanation: A bunt is a hit where the batter does not swing. Instead, the batter holds the bat still over the plate and lets the ball hit it, so the ball rolls slowly into fair territory. Teams bunt to move a runner to the next base, to surprise the defense when the infielders are playing deep, or to help a fast runner reach first base. Bunting looks easy but it is a skill with its own checkpoints.

The first move is to get into position early, as the pitcher starts the delivery. The simplest way is to pivot: keep the feet where they are and turn on the balls of both feet so the chest faces the pitcher, knees bent, bottom down a little. Some coaches teach squaring around by stepping the back foot up even with the front foot; either is fine as long as the batter stays in the batter's box and the feet are set before the ball is released. Check your league's current Little League rulebook for where the feet may be at contact.

The hands slide apart. The bottom hand stays near the knob. The top hand slides up to about the middle of the bat, just behind the start of the barrel, and pinches the bat between the thumb and the side of the bent index finger, so the fingers are folded behind the bat and never wrapped around the front where the ball could hit them. The bat is held out in front of the body with the arms relaxed and slightly bent, and the barrel is a little higher than the knob so the ball is pushed down toward the ground.

Hold the bat at the top of the strike zone, around the letters, and keep the eyes level with the bat. If the pitch is lower, bend the knees to bring the bat down with the body rather than dropping the bat head, which pops the ball up. If the pitch is above the bat, let it go; it is a ball. At contact, the hands give back an inch or two, like catching an egg, to deaden the ball so it does not roll to a fielder.

Direction comes from the bat angle, not the arms. To bunt toward third base, a right-handed batter pulls the knob back toward the body so the barrel points a little toward first; the ball comes off the bat toward third. To bunt toward first, the knob is pushed forward so the barrel angles toward third. Aim to have the ball die ten to fifteen feet up the line, between the pitcher and the baseman, where nobody can reach it quickly.
parentInstructions: Stand behind your child and to the open side for the no-ball pivot work. When you toss, you toss underhand from eight to ten feet with a soft ball and from behind an L-screen or a kneeling position off to the side; bunted balls travel slowly, but a popped-up bunt or a missed bunt can still come straight back, so never stand in front with a hard ball.

Check the top hand every time. Look for the pinch: thumb on top, bent index finger behind the bat, no fingers showing in front of the barrel. This is the one thing you must not let slide, because it is a finger safety issue.
Watch the barrel height compared to the knob. The barrel should be a little higher. A barrel that drops below the hands pops the ball up.
Watch the knees on low tosses. Your child should bend the knees to lower the whole body, not reach down with the bat.
Toss in sets of eight with a minute of rest and vary the height. Twenty-four tosses is plenty for one session.
Use a soft or tennis ball at home. A bunt is a catch with the bat, so even a soft ball teaches the give at contact perfectly.
Celebrate bunts that stop within fifteen feet up either line, and pick a target with a glove or cone so your child has something to aim for.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Use a broom handle or a short stick and a rolled sock ball tossed underhand from six feet. The pivot, the pinch grip, and the give at contact can all be practiced indoors this way.
steps: Clear twelve feet around the hitter and set a plate marker. Helmet on. Put a glove or cone fifteen feet up each imaginary baseline as targets.
With no ball, practice the pivot ten times: turn on the balls of both feet until the chest faces the pitcher, knees bent, bat out front at the top of the zone.
Practice the hand slide ten times: top hand slides up behind the barrel and pinches with the thumb and bent index finger, bottom hand stays at the knob. Parent checks for no fingers in front.

The tosser kneels eight to ten feet away, off to the side or behind a screen, and tosses eight soft balls underhand at chest height. The hitter catches each one on the bat with a small give and lets it drop.
Toss eight more, mixing heights. The hitter bends the knees for low tosses and lets high ones go.
Toss eight with the hitter angling the bat to send the ball toward the third-base target, then eight toward the first-base target.
Finish with a game: three bunts each direction, one point for each ball that stops inside fifteen feet of the plate near the target.

commonMistakes.mistake: Fingers wrapped around the front of the bat where the ball can hit them.
commonMistakes.fix: Stop and reset the pinch grip with the thumb on top and the index finger folded behind the bat. Practice ten hand slides with no ball before tossing again.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping the barrel below the hands on low pitches and popping the ball up.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child bend the knees to lower the body and keep the barrel above the knob. Toss five low balls in a row and only count the ones bunted downward.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stabbing or pushing at the ball so it rolls hard to a fielder.
commonMistakes.fix: Say 'catch it with the bat' and have the hands give back an inch at contact. Toss a few balls the child catches on the bat and lets drop at their feet.

commonMistakes.mistake: Squaring around late, after the ball is already on the way.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the tosser raise the ball slowly before each toss and require the pivot to be done by the time the ball is at its highest point.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bunting at pitches above the bat and popping them up.
commonMistakes.fix: Set the bat at the top of the zone and make a rule: if the ball is above the bat, let it go. Praise every high toss the child takes.

cues: Bend the knees, not the bat
Angle the bat, not the arms
safety: The top hand pinches the bat behind the barrel with no fingers in front. The parent checks this before every set because a tossed ball can hit exposed fingers.
Tossers kneel off to the side or behind an L-screen, eight to ten feet away, and use soft or tennis balls at home. Hard baseballs are tossed for bunting only by a coach behind a screen.
The hitter wears a batting helmet for every toss, and anyone waiting stands behind the hitter.
Indoors or in a garage, bunting is done only with sponge or tennis balls, with the hitter at least twelve feet from walls and nothing breakable in front.

progression.easier: Practice the pivot and the pinch grip with no ball, then catch tossed sponge balls on the bat and let them drop with no direction target.
progression.harder: Move to overhand coach pitch or a pitching machine from behind a screen, bunting toward a called direction, and add a timed run to first base after the bunt.

items.title: The Two-Strike Approach
items.objective: The player will be able to change their approach with two strikes by choking up, widening the stance, shortening the swing, expanding the zone slightly, and putting any strike in play.
items.summary: With two strikes the job changes from driving the ball to not striking out. This lesson gives hitters a concrete two-strike plan they can use in every at-bat.

video.note: A thirteen-year-old works a simulated 1-2 count against a coach throwing from behind an L-screen, choking up and widening the stance between pitches, fouling off a tough pitch, and then lining a single the other way.

explanation: A count is the number of balls and strikes on the batter, said balls first. At 0-2 or 1-2 or 2-2 or 3-2 the batter has two strikes, and one more strike ends the at-bat. A two-strike approach is a deliberate set of changes a hitter makes so that a borderline pitch gets fouled off or put in play instead of taken for strike three or missed. Good hitters at every level strike out less because they have a two-strike plan and use it every time.

The physical changes are small and specific. Choke up on the bat about an inch, which makes the bat quicker and easier to control. Widen the stance by two or three inches, which shortens the stride to almost nothing and keeps the head still. Move an inch or two closer to the plate so the outside corner is reachable, and bring the hands a little closer to the body so the swing is shorter. Each change by itself is tiny; together they trade a little power for a lot of contact.

The mental changes matter just as much. With fewer than two strikes a hitter looks for a pitch in a favorite spot and lets everything else go. With two strikes the zone expands slightly: anything close enough that the umpire might call a strike gets swung at. The goal shifts from hitting the ball hard to hitting the ball somewhere, ideally up the middle or to the opposite field. A hitter who tries to pull a two-strike pitch is usually fooled by anything off-speed.

A good two-strike thought is to think middle-away and let the ball travel. By looking for the ball over the outer half and waiting a split second longer, the hitter stays back on off-speed pitches and can still react inside with the shorter, quicker swing. Hitters should aim their two-strike swings at the second baseman or shortstop area, depending on which side they bat from, which keeps the barrel in the zone longer.

Fouling pitches off is a win with two strikes. A hitter who fouls off three tough pitches and then gets a mistake to hit has beaten the pitcher. Players ages eleven to sixteen should practice two-strike at-bats in front toss and batting practice with a real count, so that choking up and widening out feels normal in a game and not like giving up. Check your league's current Little League rulebook for any special rules about dropped third strikes and foul bunts with two strikes.
parentInstructions: You are the tosser for this lesson, so you must throw from behind an L-screen from eighteen to twenty-five feet, underhand or easy overhand. With a hitter this age the ball comes off the bat hard enough to hurt, so no screen means tennis balls only.
Before each set, announce the count, such as 'one and two'. Watch your child make the physical changes before you throw: hands choked up, stance wider, closer to the plate.
Mix your tosses on purpose. Throw some on the outside corner, some a little off the plate, and a couple of slower ones. Call a pitch a strike if it is close, the way an umpire would.
Count outcomes instead of hits: a foul ball, a ball put in play, or a take on a clear ball are all wins. A swing and miss or a take on a strike is a loss. Keep the score out loud.
Work in sets of six pitches as separate two-strike at-bats, with a minute to collect balls between sets. Four sets is a full session.
Ask your child where they were looking on each pitch. 'Middle-away' is the answer you want to hear most often.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Practice the two-strike setup as shadow work: from a normal stance, choke up, widen, move closer, and take a short swing on a called pitch location, repeating the change until it takes less than three seconds.
steps: Set up on a field or large park with at least sixty feet of clear space in front of the hitter. L-screen at eighteen to twenty-five feet, helmet on the hitter, everyone else behind the hitter or well behind the screen.
Take five normal swings off tosses with a zero-strike approach, looking for a pitch in a favorite spot.
The tosser calls 'one and two'. The hitter chokes up an inch, widens the stance two or three inches, and moves an inch closer to the plate. Take five shadow swings to feel the shorter stroke.
The tosser throws six pitches as one simulated at-bat, mixing locations and speeds. The hitter fouls off or puts in play every strike and takes clear balls. Keep score out loud.
Collect balls together. Discuss the one pitch that gave the most trouble and where the hitter was looking.
Run three more six-pitch two-strike at-bats, aiming balls in play at the middle of the field or the opposite field.
Finish with a set where the hitter alternates: one at-bat with a normal approach and one with two strikes, so the switch between them becomes automatic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking a borderline pitch on the corner for strike three.
commonMistakes.fix: Make a rule for the session: with two strikes, anything within a ball's width of the plate gets a swing. Count fouls as wins so swinging at close pitches feels safe.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging just as hard with two strikes and missing off-speed pitches.
commonMistakes.fix: Choke up and shorten the swing until the hitter can hit three slow tosses in a row to the opposite field, then mix speeds again.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to change the setup because the count is not announced.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the hitter say the count out loud before every pitch and make the physical changes part of a quick routine: tap the plate, choke up, widen, look middle-away.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to pull the ball with two strikes and rolling over to the pull side.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a target cone in the opposite-field gap and award two points for any ball hit toward it during two-strike at-bats.

safety: Any adult or player tossing to hitters ages eleven to sixteen is behind an L-screen. Without a screen, only tennis balls or sponge balls are used at twenty feet or more.
The hitter wears a batting helmet, and all other players stand behind the hitter outside the bat zone, never beside the screen or in the field of play.
Use a field or park with sixty feet or more of clear space; two-strike swings still produce line drives.

progression.easier: Run two-strike at-bats off a tee or side soft toss with the hitter only practicing the setup changes and a short swing, no called balls and strikes.
progression.harder: Add a runner on base and a defensive situation, so the two-strike at-bat also has a productive-out goal, as taught in the next lesson.

items.title: Hitting Behind the Runner and Productive Outs
items.objective: The player will be able to read the base-out situation before the at-bat and deliberately hit a ground ball or fly ball to the side of the field that advances the runner, even when it means making an out.
items.summary: Sometimes the best at-bat is an out that moves a teammate ninety feet closer to scoring. This lesson teaches hitters to recognize those moments and to steer the ball to the right side on purpose.

video.note: A runner on second with nobody out as a fourteen-year-old right-handed hitter lets an outside pitch travel and grounds it to the second baseman, the runner moves to third, and a diagram overlay explains why the out was productive.

explanation: Baseball is a team game, and the hitter's job changes depending on where the runners are and how many outs there are. A productive out is an out that still helps the team, usually by moving a runner to the next base or scoring a runner from third. Hitting behind the runner means hitting the ball to the right side of the field, toward first and second base, when a runner is on second, so the runner can advance to third while the fielders are busy with the ball on the other side of the diamond.

The situations to recognize are simple to list. Runner on second with nobody out: a ground ball to the right side moves the runner to third, where a fly ball or another ground ball can score him. Runner on third with fewer than two outs and the infield playing back: a ground ball up the middle or a fly ball deep enough to the outfield scores the run. Runner on first with nobody out: a ground ball to the right side can move the runner to second and stay out of the double play. Before stepping in, the hitter checks the runners, the outs, and where the infielders are standing.

Steering the ball to the right side is a contact-point skill from the tee lessons. A right-handed hitter lets the ball travel deeper and hits it to the opposite field by looking for a pitch on the outer half, keeping the hands inside, and driving the barrel toward the second baseman. A left-handed hitter pulls the ball to the right side by getting the barrel out front on a pitch on the inner half. Either way, the hitter picks the pitch that is easiest to send that direction and takes pitches that are not, unless there are two strikes.

Hitting the ball on the ground is also a choice. To keep the ball down, the hitter aims for the top half of the ball, stays short to it, and thinks about hitting a hard ground ball through the spot where the second baseman started. A fly ball to the right side is also fine with a runner on third, because the runner can tag up and score, but a pop-up to the infield helps nobody. The best productive outs are hard ground balls and deep fly balls; the worst are weak pop-ups and strikeouts.

Older Little League players should talk about these situations in the dugout and practice them with a real count and a pretend runner. Coaches will sometimes give a sign for a specific job, such as a bunt or a hit-and-run; when no sign is given, the hitter uses this lesson to pick the right job on their own. Check your league's current Little League rulebook for rules about leading off and stealing in your division, because those rules change which productive outs are possible.
parentInstructions: Throw from behind an L-screen at twenty to twenty-five feet, underhand or easy overhand, with soft baseballs or tennis balls. A hitter this age drives the ball hard enough that a screen is not optional.
Before each set, describe a situation out loud: 'runner on second, nobody out' or 'runner on third, one out, infield back'. Ask your child what the job is before you throw a pitch.

Set two cones on the field to mark the right side of the infield, between first and second base, and watch whether the ball goes between them. The result you want is a hard ground ball or deep fly ball to that side.
Notice which pitches your child swings at. Taking an inside pitch with a runner on second and nobody out is a good decision, even though it looks passive.
Run sets of six pitches as one situation, with a minute between sets to collect balls and talk about the choices. Four or five situations is a full session.
Ask your child to explain why the out mattered after each good productive out. If they can explain it, they will do it in a game without being told.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Talk through situations with a drawn diamond on paper or chalk, have the child point to where the ball should go, then take shadow swings aimed at that spot with the contact point adjusted to match.
steps: Set up on a field with bases or cones marking the infield. L-screen at twenty to twenty-five feet, helmet on, everyone else behind the hitter or well behind the screen. Mark the right-side target zone with two cones.
The tosser announces 'runner on second, nobody out'. The hitter says the job out loud: ground ball to the right side.
Toss six pitches, mixing inside and outside. The hitter takes inside pitches and drives outside pitches to the right-side zone on the ground. Count how many land in the zone.
Change the situation to 'runner on third, one out, infield back'. The hitter's job is a ground ball up the middle or a fly ball to the outfield. Toss six pitches.
Change to 'runner on first, nobody out'. The hitter looks for a pitch to hit on the ground to the right side, staying out of the double play. Toss six pitches.
Add two strikes to the last situation so the hitter must combine the two-strike approach with the productive-out goal. Toss six pitches.
Finish by having the hitter call the situation and the job without help for a final six pitches, then review how many productive results came from the whole session.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to pull every pitch regardless of where the runner is.
commonMistakes.fix: Make the right-side zone the only place a ball counts for the whole session. Have the hitter say 'other way' before each pitch and look for the outside half.

commonMistakes.mistake: Popping the ball up in the infield when trying to hit a fly ball to score the runner from third.
commonMistakes.fix: Aim for a line drive to the outfield rather than a fly ball; a hard line drive that carries is the deep fly ball you want. Think top half of the ball, not under it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging at an inside pitch with a runner on second and nobody out and grounding to the left side.
commonMistakes.fix: Practice taking three inside tosses in a row on purpose, then driving the fourth, outside toss to the right side. Taking the wrong pitch is part of the skill.

commonMistakes.mistake: Not knowing the situation before stepping into the box.
commonMistakes.fix: Build a routine: before every at-bat, look at the bases, count the outs on the fingers, and say the job in one sentence.

cues: Know the job before you step in
safety: All tossing to hitters ages eleven to sixteen is done from behind an L-screen, with soft baseballs or tennis balls when a hard ball is not needed.
This lesson belongs on a full field or a large park with ninety feet of clear space to the right side, since the goal is to hit the ball into the infield.

The hitter wears a batting helmet, waiting players stand behind the hitter, and any player acting as a pretend fielder on the right side wears a glove and stays on the outfield grass beyond the cones.

progression.easier: Work one situation only, runner on second and nobody out, off a tee set on the outside corner so the hitter can groove the opposite-field ground ball before adding a tosser.
progression.harder: Add live fielders and a baserunner to each situation, and let the coach give signs so the hitter must combine reading the situation with following a bunt or hit-and-run call.

items.title: From Tee Ball to Coach Pitch: Hitting a Moving Ball
items.objective: The player will be able to track a soft ball pitched overhand by a coach from about twenty feet, start the swing on time, and make contact on at least half of the strikes in a set of ten.
items.summary: The jump from a still ball on a tee to a ball thrown by a coach is the biggest change a young hitter faces. This lesson breaks it into small steps so the swing stays the same while the ball starts to move.

video.note: A seven-year-old progresses through four clips in one session: tee hits, side soft toss, underhand front toss, and finally overhand coach pitch from twenty feet, with the swing staying the same and the camera highlighting the eyes tracking the ball.

explanation: In tee ball the ball sits still and the hitter can take all the time in the world. In coach pitch a grown-up throws the ball from about twenty feet away, and it arrives in less than a second. The swing does not need to change at all. What changes is that the hitter now has to see the ball coming, decide if it is a good one, and start the swing at the right moment. Those three things, seeing, deciding, and timing, are what this lesson practices.

Seeing comes first. The hitter watches the coach's throwing hand from the moment the coach lifts the ball. The eyes follow the ball out of the hand, through the air, and all the way to the bat. Children who look at the coach's face or at the field will miss, because the ball is small and fast and the eyes must be on it early. Playing the color-call game from the tracking lesson with the coach pitching, where the child calls the color of a dot on the ball, is a great way to check.

Deciding means swinging only at good pitches. A good pitch is one that would cross the plate between the hitter's knees and chest. Coach pitch leagues often allow a set number of pitches per batter, so hitters should not swing at balls over their head or in the dirt. A simple rule for seven- and eight-year-olds is: if the ball is coming to your belly, swing; if it is not, let it go and get ready for the next one. Check your league's current Little League rulebook for the pitch count per batter and whether a tee is used after a set number of misses.

Timing means starting the swing early enough. The load, the little move back from the earlier lessons, starts when the coach's arm goes up. The stride foot lands as the ball leaves the hand, and then the hitter swings. Young hitters who wait until the ball is close before moving will always be late, and late swings miss or foul the ball off. Starting early and being ready to swing is the whole secret.

The way to teach all of this is a ladder. Hit five balls off the tee to warm up the swing, then five side soft tosses so the ball moves a little. Hit five underhand front tosses from fifteen feet so the ball comes from the pitcher's direction, then ten overhand coach pitches from about twenty feet with a soft ball. Any time swings fall apart, step back one rung and climb again. Most children get there in a few weeks of short sessions with a lot of praise.
parentInstructions: You will be the pitcher, so you need protection. Throw from behind an L-screen if you have one. If you do not, use only soft safety balls or sponge balls and throw from about twenty feet, which is also the typical coach-pitch distance; the ball can come back at you.

Throw overhand with an easy, slow, repeatable motion. Lift the ball high so your child can see it, then throw at a speed where the ball arcs gently to belt height. Accuracy matters far more than speed; aim for the belly every time.
Say 'ready' before each pitch and wait until your child is in the stance with eyes on your hand. Never throw to a child who is looking somewhere else.
Watch the eyes and the start of the load. If your child does not move until the ball is halfway, say 'start when my arm goes up' before the next pitch.
Throw in sets of ten pitches with a rest to collect balls together. Three sets of ten is the maximum for a seven-year-old, and finish early if focus fades.
Count contact, not hits. A foul tip counts as contact. Say the running total out loud so your child hears progress.
Keep everybody else behind the hitter. Siblings who want to help can stand behind you, well behind the screen, and hand you balls.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Pitch a rolled sock ball or a crumpled paper ball underhand from ten feet in the yard while the child swings a plastic bat or a broom handle. The ball moves slowly enough to practice eyes, decision, and timing without any real equipment.
steps: Set up on a field or large yard with forty feet of clear space in front of the hitter. The hitter wears a helmet and anyone watching stays behind the hitter and outside the bat zone. Set the L-screen or decide on sponge balls.
Hit five balls off the tee to warm up the swing, freezing the finish each time.
Move to side soft toss into open space or a net: five tosses from the open side, ten feet away and a step ahead of the plate.
Move to underhand front toss from fifteen feet, from behind the screen: five tosses, with the hitter loading as the hand drops.
Throw three overhand coach pitches with no swing allowed. The hitter tracks each ball to the plate and says 'yes' if it was a good pitch or 'no' if it was not.
Throw ten overhand coach pitches at an easy speed. The hitter swings only at pitches coming to the belly. Count contact out loud.
Rest, collect balls together, and throw a second set of ten. Finish with three tee balls so the last swing of the day is a good one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging late at every pitch because the load does not start until the ball is close.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child say 'go' out loud when your arm goes up, and start the load on that word. Throw three pitches with no swing just to practice the early start.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging at everything, including balls over the head and in the dirt.
commonMistakes.fix: Throw three obvious bad pitches on purpose and praise each one the child takes. Then mix good and bad pitches and keep score of good decisions.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stepping away from the plate as the ball comes, often called stepping in the bucket or bailing out, because the moving ball is scary.
commonMistakes.fix: Go back to sponge balls and shorter distances for a week, and let the child stand behind a fence while you throw a few pitches so they can watch the ball without worrying about being hit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Looking at the parent's face instead of the throwing hand.
commonMistakes.fix: Hold the ball up high before each pitch and ask the child to point at it with the bat before getting set. Use balls with colored dots and have them call the color at contact.

commonMistakes.mistake: Losing the tee swing once the ball moves and swinging with all arms.
commonMistakes.fix: Step back down the ladder to the tee for three swings, then soft toss, then return to coach pitch. The swing should look the same at every rung.

cues: Start when the arm goes up
safety: Children ages seven and eight hit only soft or safety balls when a ball is pitched at home. Hard baseballs are not pitched to children this age in practice.
The hitter wears a batting helmet for every pitch and toss. All other children stand behind the hitter and outside the bat zone.
The adult pitching stands behind an L-screen, or uses sponge or safety balls from twenty feet if no screen is available, and never pitches to a child who is not looking.
Use a field, park, or large yard with at least forty feet of open space in front of the hitter and nothing breakable in the flight path.

progression.easier: Stay on the ladder rungs of tee and side soft toss for the whole session, or throw underhand coach pitch from fifteen feet before trying overhand.
progression.harder: Add a pitch count like a game, five or six pitches per at-bat, and have the child run to first base after a hit. Mix in slightly faster pitches once contact is steady.
